title: Parasites and hosts: an arms race, and parasites who change what a host does

summary.text: A praying mantis lives on bushes and keeps away from water. Yet a mantis with a hairworm inside walks to a pond and steps in. Why would any animal do that? In this lesson you will run a pond of seed snails for eight generations and find out why the best-protected snail does not stay the best. You will learn how parasites and hosts keep answering each other's moves, and how some parasites change what a host does.
summary.art: A green praying mantis standing at the edge of a village pond at sunset, looking at the shining water, with a hibiscus bush behind.

intro.hook: A rat who smells a cat runs away. A rat who carries a certain parasite in the brain walks towards the smell. Who gains from that walk?
intro.text: A parasite is a living being who lives on or inside another living being, the host, and takes food from them. The host fights back. Then the parasite changes, and the host has to change again. This goes on for millions of years, and scientists call it an arms race. Some parasites have gone further. They change what the host does, so that the host carries them to their next home. We will test the arms race with seeds and a die. Then we will look at the evidence for parasites who steer their hosts.
intro.art: A brown rat on a kitchen floor at night walking calmly towards a sleeping cat, with a thought bubble showing a question mark.

outcomes: By the end I can say what an arms race between a parasite and a host is, and give two examples of a move and an answer.
By the end I can explain, from the Pond Race, why the commonest kind of host does not stay the best protected, and why variety protects a group.
By the end I can describe how a body learns to know a parasite, and how some parasites escape by changing their coat.
By the end I can name four parasites who change what a host does, and say who gains from each change.
By the end I can tell apart a change that helps the parasite, a change that helps the host and a side effect of illness, and say how to test which one it is.
By the end I can say which claims about parasites are tested, which are only seen, and which scientists still argue about.
By the end I can say what to do after a dog bite or scratch, and how to keep safe from parasites carried by cats and soil.

terms.meaning: A living being who lives on or inside another living being and takes food from them. The parasite gains and the other one loses something.
terms.example: A head louse on a scalp, a malaria parasite in the blood and a hairworm inside a mantis are all parasites.
terms.art: Three small circles showing a louse on a hair, tiny ring shapes inside red blood cells, and a thin dark worm coiled inside the outline of a mantis.

terms.meaning: The living being that a parasite lives on or in. The host gives the parasite food and a home, without choosing to.
terms.example: A person is the host of a head louse. A snail is the host of a young fluke.
terms.art: A snail on a wet leaf with a small arrow pointing inside the shell, where tiny worm shapes are drawn.

terms.meaning: A long contest in which two sides keep answering each other's changes. Each new defence is followed by a new way round it.
terms.example: Reed warblers learned to throw out strange eggs. Cuckoos now lay eggs that look like reed warbler eggs.
terms.art: A staircase drawn from the side with a small bird on one step and a larger bird on the next step, each step higher than the last.

terms.meaning: Two kinds of living beings changing over many generations because of each other. An arms race is one kind of coevolution.
terms.example: Snails and the flukes who infect them have changed together for a very long time.
terms.art: Two wavy lines that cross each other again and again across a page, one labelled snails and one labelled flukes.

terms.meaning: All the young born at about the same time. Parents are one generation and their children are the next.
terms.example: You, your parents and your grandparents are three generations.
terms.art: Three rows of snails, one above the other, with arrows from each row to the row below.

terms.meaning: The small differences between living beings of one kind. Many of these differences are passed from parents to young.
terms.example: Children in one class differ in height, in blood group and in which illnesses they catch easily.
terms.art: A row of eight snails of one kind, each with a slightly different pattern on the shell.

terms.meaning: What happens when some living beings leave more young than others because of how they are built. Their kind becomes more common in the next generation.
terms.example: Flukes who fit the commonest snail find more hosts and leave more young.
terms.art: Two bowls of seeds, the first with a few green seeds among many red ones and the second, labelled later, with mostly green seeds.

terms.meaning: A living being who is an exact copy of their one parent. A group of clones has almost no variation.
terms.example: Some New Zealand mud snails are clones. A mother snail has daughters without a father, and each daughter is a copy of her.
terms.art: One snail with five smaller snails around her, all with exactly the same shell pattern.

terms.meaning: The protection that a kind of host gets from being uncommon. Few parasites fit a rare kind, because parasites who fit the common kind do better.
terms.example: In the Pond Race, the kind of snail with the fewest seeds was infected least often.
terms.art: A crowd of red snails with many small flukes swimming towards them, and one green snail at the side with no flukes near.

terms.meaning: The idea that living beings must keep changing only to stay as well off as before, because their enemies are changing too.
terms.example: In a story by Lewis Carroll, the Red Queen tells Alice that here you must run as fast as you can just to stay in the same place.
terms.art: A girl and a chess queen running hand in hand on a chessboard field while the trees beside them stay in the same place.

terms.meaning: All the parts of a body that find and fight germs and parasites. It includes skin, special blood cells and the chemicals they make.
terms.example: When a cut gets red and warm, cells of the immune system have arrived to fight microbes.
terms.art: An outline of a child's body with small shield shapes in the blood, the skin, the gut and the throat.

terms.meaning: A tiny Y-shaped protein that the body makes to grip one particular germ or parasite. Each antibody fits one shape only.
terms.example: After chickenpox, the body keeps cells that can quickly make chickenpox antibodies again.
terms.art: Several Y shapes gripping the bumps on the surface of a round parasite.

terms.meaning: The outer layer of proteins on a parasite. It is the part that the host's antibodies learn to grip.
terms.example: A sleeping-sickness parasite is covered in millions of copies of one coat protein.
terms.art: A long wavy single-celled parasite drawn with a thick outline made of many small identical beads.

terms.meaning: A parasite switching to a different coat protein, so that the antibodies made for the old coat no longer fit. Scientists call it antigenic variation.
terms.example: Sleeping-sickness parasites carry about two thousand coat genes and use one at a time.
terms.art: The same wavy parasite drawn three times in a row, each time with beads of a different colour, and Y shapes that fit only the first.

terms.meaning: The ability of a germ or parasite to survive a medicine that used to kill their kind.
terms.example: Many malaria parasites are now resistant to the old medicine chloroquine.
terms.art: A tablet strip beside a blood drop in which a few ring-shaped parasites remain while the others have faded.

terms.meaning: A bird who lays her eggs in the nest of another kind of bird. The other bird then feeds her chick.
terms.example: The Asian koel lays her eggs in the nests of house crows.
terms.art: A crow's stick nest in a neem tree with four pale green eggs and one slightly smaller egg.

terms.meaning: The host in which a parasite becomes an adult and has young. Many parasites must reach one particular final host.
terms.example: Toxoplasma can live in many animals, but has young by mating only inside cats.
terms.art: A cat sitting beside a small arrow that points from a rat to the cat.

terms.meaning: A change in what a host does that is caused by a parasite and that helps the parasite to spread or to reach the next host.
terms.example: A mantis with a full-grown hairworm inside walks into water, where the worm needs to be.
terms.art: A mantis stepping into a pond while a thin worm shape is drawn inside her body in a lighter colour.

terms.meaning: A change that comes with being ill but helps nobody in particular. It is not a defence and not a trick.
terms.example: An animal with many worms may move slowly only because the worms have taken much of the food.
terms.art: A thin, tired goat lying down in the shade while other goats graze.

terms.meaning: A deadly disease caused by a virus in the saliva of an infected animal. The virus reaches the brain and changes how the animal behaves.
terms.example: In India most people who get rabies got the virus from a dog bite. Washing the wound and a vaccine given in time prevent the disease.
terms.art: A child washing a small bite mark on the leg under a running tap with a bar of soap, while a grown-up looks at a clock.

terms.meaning: The part of a test where nothing is changed, so that there is something to compare with.
terms.example: In the Starling Test, the round with all the paper bugs hidden is the control.
terms.art: Two trays side by side, one labelled test and one labelled control, with the same paper circles on each.

explanations.concept: An arms race: a move, an answer, and another move
explanations.definition: An arms race is a contest between two kinds of living beings in which each change on one side is followed, over generations, by a change on the other side.
explanations.description: A parasite takes food from a host, so a host who can keep parasites out leaves more young. That is why hosts have defences such as skin, grooming and an immune system. But a parasite who cannot get past the defence leaves no young at all. So any parasite who is born a little different, and gets through, has many young. After some generations most parasites can get through, and the host's defence is worth less. Now any host who is born with a new defence does well. The contest has no finish line. Nobody plans the moves ahead. Each move is a small difference that some were born with, and that helped them to leave more young. The name arms race was first used for countries that keep building more weapons because the other country does.
examples: A louse has claws that grip one hair. People answer with fine combs. Lice in many places are now resistant to common lice lotions.
Reed warblers in Europe throw out eggs that look unlike their own. Cuckoos who use reed warbler nests lay eggs that look like reed warbler eggs.

Bacteria are attacked by viruses. Many bacteria keep small pieces of old viruses in their own genes, and use them to recognise and cut the same virus next time. Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna turned this defence, called CRISPR, into a tool for changing genes.
explanations.art: A zigzag path climbing a hill, with a small snail drawn at each turn on the left and a small fluke at each turn on the right.

explanations.concept: How a change spreads without anyone planning it
explanations.definition: Natural selection means that the living beings whose bodies suit their surroundings leave more young, so their kind becomes more common.
explanations.description: Three things are needed. First, the members of one kind differ a little from each other. This is variation. Second, some of those differences are passed to the young. Third, some differences change how many young survive. Put these together and the group changes from one generation to the next. In the Pond Race you did not tell any fluke to change. You only let the flukes who found a snail have more young than the flukes who did not. The fluke card changed all the same. For parasites this happens fast, because many parasites have a new generation in days or weeks, and one host may have a new generation only after many years. This is one reason hosts can never win the race for good.
examples: Chloroquine once cured almost all malaria. A few parasites had a small change in one gene that kept the medicine away from where it works. They survived, and their young filled the place of the others.
In your Pond Race, the fluke who fitted the commonest snail took four squares of the card after one generation.
explanations.art: Three bowls in a row showing the same mix of seeds changing: mostly red, then half red and half green, then mostly green.

explanations.concept: Lock and key: why a parasite fits some hosts and not others
explanations.definition: A parasite gets into a host's cell, or hides from the host's defences, only when molecules on the parasite fit molecules on the host.
explanations.description: Every cell is covered in proteins. A protein is a long chain of atoms folded into one exact shape. A parasite also carries proteins on the outside. To enter a cell, a protein on the parasite must fit a protein on the cell, somewhat as a key fits a lock. If the shapes do not fit, the parasite stays outside. The shape of each protein is written in a gene, and genes differ a little from one snail to the next. So one fluke may fit one family of snails well and another family badly. This is a simplified picture. Real infection takes many steps, with many locks and keys, and scientists have worked out the exact molecules for only some parasites. In the Pond Race we used three kinds of seed to stand for three kinds of lock.
examples: One kind of malaria parasite, Plasmodium vivax, enters a red blood cell by gripping a protein called Duffy. Most people in West and Central Africa lack that protein on their red cells, and this malaria is rare there.
A dog flea and a cat flea can each bite a person, but a head louse from a person cannot live on a dog. The fit is close.
explanations.art: A zoomed-in drawing of the surface of a round cell with three differently shaped notches, and a parasite whose bump fits only one notch.

explanations.concept: Why the commonest kind does not stay on top
explanations.definition: When parasites fit one kind of host at a time, the commonest kind of host is attacked most and a rare kind is attacked least. This is called rare advantage.
explanations.description: Think about a fluke looking for a snail. If most snails in the pond are of one kind, a fluke who fits that kind finds a host easily and has many young. A fluke who fits a rare kind mostly meets the wrong snails. So after a few generations, most flukes fit the commonest snail. Now the commonest snails are infected most, and have fewer young. A rare kind is hardly touched, has many young, and becomes common. Then the flukes who fit that kind do well, and it begins again. Curtis Lively, Mark Dybdahl and Jukka Jokela watched this in a lake in New Zealand. The snails there are attacked by a fluke who stops an infected snail from having young. Over 7 to 10 years, the commonest families of clone snails were almost completely replaced by families that had been rare. In a laboratory, Britt Koskella and Curtis Lively showed that the commonest kind of snail went down only in tanks that had flukes.
examples: In the Pond Race, rajma snails began with 8 of the 12 places and usually lost the lead within a few generations.
Farmers who plant one variety of a crop over a huge area sometimes lose the whole crop to one disease. Mixed fields usually lose less.
explanations.art: A line graph with three coloured lines that rise and fall in turn, each line peaking just after another has fallen.

explanations.concept: The Red Queen: is this why living beings mix their genes?
explanations.definition: The Red Queen idea says that living beings must keep changing just to stay as safe as before, because their parasites and other enemies keep changing too.
explanations.description: Leigh Van Valen gave the idea its name in 1973, from the Red Queen in Lewis Carroll's book Through the Looking-Glass. Other scientists then used it for a hard question. A mother who makes copies of herself, as a clone snail does, has twice as many daughters as a mother who needs a father for her young. So why do most animals and plants need two parents? One answer is parasites. Young with two parents get a fresh mix of genes, so many of them are a rare kind that few parasites fit. In your second pond, the clone snails had no rare kind to fall back on. Scientists agree that this happens in some animals. They do not agree that it is the main reason for two parents everywhere.
examples: In New Zealand lakes, snails with two parents are more common in the shallow water, where the flukes are common.
The clone pond in the Pond Race usually shrank to a few snails or none in eight generations.

perspectives.who: William Hamilton, Curtis Lively and others
perspectives.explanation: Parasites are the main reason. They change so fast that a host family must keep making new mixes of genes or be caught.
Mixing genes mainly helps to get rid of harmful mistakes in genes. Young who get many mistakes die, and the mistakes go with them.
Both matter, and their share differs from one kind of living being to another. Some clones have lasted a very long time, and nobody is sure how.

explanations.art: Two ponds side by side, one with snails of many shell patterns and one with snails that all look the same, with small flukes swimming in both.

explanations.concept: How a body learns to know a parasite
explanations.definition: The immune system is the body's defence. One part of it acts at once against anything strange. Another part learns the exact shape of each invader and remembers it.
explanations.description: The first part is fast and general. Skin keeps most things out. Certain white blood cells swallow microbes, and the body may raise its temperature, which is a fever. The second part is slower and exact. White blood cells called B cells each make one shape of antibody. An antibody is a Y-shaped protein whose tips grip one shape and nothing else. When a B cell's antibody happens to fit a new parasite, that cell divides into thousands of copies, and they pour out antibodies. This takes one to two weeks the first time. Antibodies stick to the parasite and mark them for other cells to destroy. Some of the B cells stay for years as memory cells, so the second meeting is answered in days. A vaccine works by giving the body this first meeting safely. Notice that the same three things are at work as in natural selection: many different cells, one that fits, and many copies of the one that fits. This time it happens inside one body, in days.
examples: A child who has had measles, or the measles vaccine, almost never gets measles again.
People who grow up where malaria is common get milder malaria as adults, because their bodies have met many coats of the parasite.
explanations.art: A row of white blood cells each holding up a differently shaped Y, with one Y fitting the bump on a parasite and that cell splitting into many copies.

explanations.concept: Coat changers: parasites who cannot be learned
explanations.definition: Some parasites keep ahead of antibodies by changing the proteins on their surface. Scientists call this antigenic variation.
explanations.description: The parasite of sleeping sickness in Africa is a single cell called a trypanosome, who lives in the blood. They are covered in a thick coat made of millions of copies of one protein. The body learns that coat and kills nearly all the parasites. But the parasite carries about two thousand genes and pieces of genes for other coats, and uses one at a time. Now and then one parasite switches to another coat. The old antibodies do not fit. That parasite multiplies, until the body learns the new coat too. So the number of parasites in the blood goes up and down in waves, and the infection can last for months or years. A malaria parasite, Plasmodium falciparum, does something similar. They put a protein on the outside of the red blood cell they live in, and they have about 60 genes for it. A relative of the sleeping-sickness parasite lives in India. Trypanosoma evansi causes a disease called surra in camels, horses and cattle, and is carried by biting flies. Griffith Evans first saw this parasite in the blood of sick horses in 1880, at Dera Ismail Khan, which is now in Pakistan.
examples: A person with sleeping sickness has fever that comes and goes as each new coat grows and is beaten.
The flu virus also changes surface proteins from year to year. That is why a flu vaccine is made new each year.
explanations.art: A graph with five humps in a row, each hump in a different colour, and above each hump a small parasite wearing a coat of that colour.

explanations.definition: When people use a medicine against a parasite, the parasites who survive the medicine leave the young. Over time the medicine works less well. This is resistance.
explanations.description: Humans have added a new kind of move to the arms race, which is medicine. Chloroquine cured malaria cheaply from the 1940s. Parasites that it could not kill were first suspected near the border of Thailand and Cambodia in 1957. In India they were first reported in 1973, in the Karbi Anglong district of Assam. In 1972 Tu Youyou and her team in China separated a new medicine, artemisinin, from the sweet wormwood plant, after reading old Chinese books of medicine. It has saved millions of lives, and she shared the Nobel Prize in 2015. In 2008 and 2009, doctors in western Cambodia found parasites that artemisinin cleared more slowly than before. So today artemisinin is always given together with a second medicine. A parasite would need to be born with the answer to both at once, and that is far less likely. This is also why a person must finish every tablet the doctor gives. Stopping early kills the easy parasites and leaves the tough ones.
examples: India's malaria programme gives artemisinin together with other medicines for falciparum malaria, never alone.
Head lice in many countries now survive lotions that killed them thirty years ago. A fine comb still works, because no louse egg can become too small for the comb quickly.
explanations.art: A strip of two different coloured tablets side by side, with a ring-shaped parasite facing two locked doors instead of one.

explanations.concept: Egg tricks: cuckoos, koels and their hosts
explanations.definition: A brood parasite is a bird who lays eggs in another bird's nest. The host bird loses food and work, and often loses chicks, so hosts have defences and brood parasites have answers.
explanations.description: In the 1980s Nick Davies and Michael Brooke put painted model eggs into reed warbler nests in England. The reed warblers accepted model eggs that looked like their own and threw out most of the others. So a cuckoo's egg must look right, and the eggs of cuckoos who use reed warblers do look like reed warbler eggs. The cuckoo also lays very quickly, while the hosts are away. In India the best-known brood parasite is the Asian koel, whose rising call you hear from March. The female koel lays in the nests of house crows and jungle crows. The koel chick does not push the crow chicks out. They grow up together. People long said that koel eggs copy crow eggs. A study in Bangladesh in 2021 measured the eggs in the way a bird's eye sees them, and found no close copying of any one host. So how crows and koels answer each other is still being worked out.
examples: The koel's egg hatches a few days sooner than the crow's eggs, so the koel chick is fed first.
The pied cuckoo, who arrives in North India before the monsoon, lays in the nests of babblers.
explanations.art: A female koel with spotted brown feathers slipping into a crow's stick nest while two crows chase a glossy black male koel in the distance.

explanations.concept: Hosts fight back with what they do
explanations.definition: Not every defence is inside the body. Many animals, including people, keep parasites away by how they behave.
explanations.description: A bird draws each feather through the beak. This is preening, and it removes lice and mites. Cows swish their tails at flies. Monkeys pick through each other's fur. Ants carry their dying and dead nest-mates far from the nest, which keeps fungus spores away from the young. Some animals even seem to treat themselves. At Mahale in Tanzania, Michael Huffman and his colleagues watched chimpanzees fold rough, hairy leaves and swallow them whole, without chewing. In the dung they found the leaves, with gut worms among them. People do all of this too. We comb, wash, cook food, wear footwear, sleep under nets and stay away from dung. Even the feeling of disgust is a defence. So a host's behaviour is also part of the arms race, and that is exactly why a parasite who can change a host's behaviour gains so much.
examples: A crow on a wire spends many minutes a day preening. Count them in the Preening Count activity.
A fever is a defence that the whole body takes part in. Many microbes grow more slowly when the body is hotter.
explanations.art: Four small scenes: a crow preening a wing feather, a cow swishing her tail, two monkeys grooming, and a child being combed by her grandmother.

explanations.concept: Parasites who change a host so that the host is eaten
explanations.definition: Many parasites must get from one kind of host into another kind that eats the first. Some of them change what the first host does, so that this host is caught more easily.
explanations.description: A worm who lives in a pill bug cannot walk to a starling. But starlings eat pill bugs. In 1983 Janice Moore found that pill bugs with this worm inside spent more time in open, dry, light places, and that starlings ate more of them. On the coast of California, a fluke forms tiny cysts on the brain of a small fish called a killifish. Kevin Lafferty and Kimo Morris found in 1996 that infected fish flash their bright sides and jerk near the surface four times as often as healthy fish. Birds, the fluke's final host, ate the infected fish 10 to 30 times as often. A single-celled parasite called Toxoplasma can live in the brain of a rat, but can mate only inside a cat. Healthy rats stay away from the smell of cat urine. Manuel Berdoy, Joanne Webster and David Macdonald showed in 2000 that infected rats lose this fear, and some even go towards the smell. In 2007 Ajai Vyas and his colleagues found that the rats' other fears stayed the same. Only the fear of cats had changed.
examples: Infected pill bugs also moved about more, so they were not simply weak.
Nobody has yet measured how many more infected rats are really caught by cats outdoors.
explanations.art: A split picture: on the left dark pill bugs hiding under a damp leaf, on the right one pill bug walking across pale dry soil with a starling looking down at her.

explanations.concept: Parasites who change a host to reach the right place
explanations.definition: Some parasites do not need the host to be eaten. They need the host to go to one particular place, at one particular time.
explanations.description: A hairworm grows inside a cricket or a praying mantis until the worm fills most of the body. But adult hairworms live and mate in water, and a mantis keeps away from water. When the worm is full grown, the mantis walks into a pond or stream, and the worm comes out. In 2021 a team in Japan found a reason. Light that bounces off flat water is polarised, which means its waves all lie flat in one direction. Mantises with a hairworm inside walked towards this kind of light. Healthy mantises did not. In forests in Thailand, Brazil and elsewhere, a fungus grows inside carpenter ants. An infected ant leaves the nest, climbs a plant, and bites hard into a vein under a leaf at about midday. The ant dies there. A stalk grows from the head and drops spores on the path below, where other ants walk. In 2017 scientists looked inside infected ants. The fungus had spread around and into the muscles all through the body, but they did not find fungus inside the brain. How the fungus steers the ant is still not known.
examples: In nine streams in Japan, crickets and their relatives made up nearly half of what the trout had in their stomachs, on average. Streams with more hairworms had trout who had eaten more of them.
In India, hairworms have been recorded from praying mantises. About twenty kinds of hairworm are known from the country so far, most from the east and north-east.
explanations.art: An ant gripping the underside of a leaf with her jaws, a thin stalk growing up from behind her head, and tiny dots falling to the forest floor.

explanations.concept: Rabies: a virus who changes how a dog behaves
explanations.definition: Rabies is a disease caused by a virus that passes in the saliva of an infected animal, usually through a bite. The virus travels to the brain and changes behaviour.
explanations.description: After a bite the virus does not go into the blood. The virus enters the nerves near the wound and moves along them towards the brain. This is slow. It usually takes two to three months, and sometimes only a week or as long as a year. Once in the brain, the virus multiplies and moves out to the salivary glands. Many infected dogs become restless and bite at things they would have left alone. The animal cannot swallow well, so saliva full of virus stays in the mouth. Each of these changes helps the virus to reach the next animal. Once signs of rabies begin in a person, the disease is almost always fatal. But it can be stopped completely in the weeks before that, because the virus travels slowly. According to the World Health Organization, dogs pass on the virus in up to 99 out of 100 human cases, about 4 in 10 deaths are children under 15, and India has about a third of the world's rabies deaths. So every child should know the steps. Wash the bite or scratch with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes. Tell a grown-up at once, even if the wound is small and even if the dog is a pet. See a doctor the same day for the vaccine, and take every dose.
examples: A lick on broken skin or a scratch from an infected animal can also pass the virus.
Putting chilli, oil or turmeric on a bite does not stop the virus. Soap and water, and then the vaccine, do.
explanations.art: A three-part strip: a child washing a bite on the calf under a tap with soap, the child telling her mother, and a nurse giving an injection in the upper arm.

explanations.concept: Trick, defence or side effect? How to tell
explanations.definition: When an infected animal behaves oddly, there are three possible reasons. The change may help the parasite, it may help the host, or it may be a side effect of illness that helps nobody.
explanations.description: A sneeze throws a cold virus across a room, and it also clears the nose. Is the sneeze the virus's trick or the body's defence? It may be both. Scientists use several tests before they call a change manipulation. First, do infected animals really behave differently from healthy ones, in a fair comparison? Second, does the change happen at the time when the parasite is ready to move on, and not before? Third, does the change really carry more parasites to the next host? Fourth, is the change exact, like losing only the fear of cats, or is the animal just slow and ill? Janice Moore's pill bugs passed these tests. Many famous stories have passed only the first one. In 2023 scientists went back to the California killifish and infected young fish on purpose. The infected fish did become more showy, so the fluke does cause the change.
examples: A lizard with a fever sits in the sun for longer. That helps the lizard, so it is a defence.
A goat with many gut worms eats less and moves slowly. That may be only a side effect.

perspectives.who: Richard Dawkins, in The Extended Phenotype (1982)
perspectives.explanation: A parasite's genes can show their effects in the host's body and behaviour. The mantis walking to water is the worm's genes at work, in the same way that a web is a spider's genes at work.

perspectives.who: Robert Poulin and other careful parasitologists
perspectives.explanation: Many changes are small, and many have never been tested against the next host. Call a change manipulation only when the tests have been done.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study the host's side
perspectives.explanation: Some changes are the host's own answer. An infected bumblebee who stays out of the nest in the cold slows the parasite down and may protect her sisters.

explanations.art: A page with three columns headed Helps the parasite, Helps the host and Helps nobody, with a sneezing child drawn across the line between the first two.

explanations.definition: Toxoplasma gondii is a single-celled parasite who can live in almost any warm-blooded animal, including people, but mates only in cats. Whether the parasite changes human behaviour is not settled.
explanations.description: A cat who catches the parasite passes tiny egg-like cysts in the dung for a short time. The cysts get into soil and water, and on to unwashed vegetables. Other animals swallow them, and the parasite forms resting cysts in muscle and brain. People also get the parasite from undercooked meat. Scientists estimate that around a third of all people carry these resting cysts, with large differences between countries. Most healthy people never feel ill. The parasite can seriously harm a baby before birth if the mother is infected for the first time while pregnant, and can harm people whose immune system is very weak. Some studies have found that infected people are a little slower to react, or have more road accidents. Other studies have found no difference. Humans are a dead end for the parasite, since cats almost never eat people today. So if there is any effect on us, it may be left over from what the parasite does in rats. To keep safe, wash your hands after touching soil, sand or a cat's litter, wash fruit and vegetables, and eat meat only when it is cooked through.
examples: A cat's litter tray should be cleaned every day, because the cysts need one to five days outside the cat before they can infect anyone.
Cats are safe to stroke. The parasite is in dung and soil, not in fur or purring.

perspectives.who: Jaroslav Flegr and some other researchers
perspectives.explanation: Infected people differ a little in reaction time and in some personality tests, and this fits what the parasite does to rats.
Large studies have not found the same differences. People who are infected may differ in other ways, such as where they live and what they eat.

explanations.art: A child washing soil off carrots at a kitchen sink while a cat sits on the windowsill behind her.

explanations.concept: How can a parasite reach into behaviour at all?
explanations.definition: Behaviour is run by signals in nerves and by chemicals in the blood. A parasite who makes or changes those chemicals can change what the host does.
explanations.description: A signal in a nerve is a wave of charged atoms, called ions, moving in and out of the nerve cell. Where one nerve cell meets the next, the signal is carried across by small molecules such as dopamine. Hormones in the blood carry slower messages, such as hunger and fear. All of these are chemicals, and any living being can make chemicals. The jewel wasp, who lives in South Asia and Africa, is the clearest case. She stings a cockroach twice. The second sting goes into the cockroach's head, and scientists have shown that her venom reaches two exact places in the brain. The cockroach can still walk, but no longer starts walking alone. The wasp leads the cockroach by one antenna to a burrow and lays an egg on them. For most other parasites we have only ideas. Hairworms make proteins that look like the insect's own brain proteins. Toxoplasma cysts were found more often in the part of the rat brain that handles fear. Nobody yet knows the full chain from a parasite's molecule to a mantis stepping into water.
examples: Caffeine in tea changes how awake you feel. It is a plant chemical that fits a lock in human nerve cells.
The rabies virus travels inside nerve cells, which is how the virus reaches the brain without being met by antibodies in the blood.
explanations.art: A zoomed-in view of the gap between two nerve cells with small dots crossing it, and a second kind of dot, coloured differently, arriving from a parasite and fitting the same slots.

explanations.definition: A parasite senses the host's body and acts on what is sensed. Parasites decide when to multiply, when to rest and when to move on.
explanations.description: Sleeping-sickness parasites sense how crowded they are in the blood. When the crowd is thick, many of them stop dividing and change into a short, stout form that waits for a tsetse fly. This keeps the host alive for longer. Malaria parasites in the blood keep time with the host's day and night. A hairworm senses when they are full grown, and only then is the mantis drawn to water. A tick waits for the smell of breath and the warmth of skin. These are living beings who take in news of their world and act on that news, which is what sensing and deciding mean. A parasite is not a simple or lower being. A fluke who passes through a snail, a fish and a bird has to solve three different bodies in one life.
examples: A young filarial worm is in the blood near the skin mostly at night, when the mosquitoes who carry them bite.
Cuckoo chicks call like a whole nest of hungry reed warbler chicks, and the foster parents bring more food.

perspectives.explanation: Sensing, choosing and acting are found in every living being, with or without a brain. A parasite does them in a parasite's way.
They call these automatic responses. In their view, genes that happened to produce the right response were kept by natural selection, and nothing is chosen.

explanations.art: A crowd of long thin single-celled parasites in a blood vessel, a few of them changing into a shorter, stouter shape.

explanations.concept: Parasites hold the web of life together
explanations.definition: Parasites are a large part of all living beings, and they shape who eats whom, who is common and who is rare.
explanations.description: It is easy to think of parasites as extras that the living world could do without. The evidence points the other way. When Kevin Lafferty and his colleagues weighed everything living in three river mouths in California and Mexico, the parasites together weighed more than all the birds. In streams in Japan, the trout ate more crickets wherever there were more hairworms, so a parasite was feeding the fish. Parasites also keep any one kind of host from taking over, as the flukes did in your pond. Some old partnerships may even have begun as a kind of infection. Lynn Margulis showed that the mitochondria who release energy in each of your cells were once free-living bacteria who moved into a larger cell. Whether they came in as food, as guests or as parasites, nobody knows. So the line between a parasite and a partner can move over time.
examples: A cuckoo, a koel, a louse, a fluke, a mistletoe on a mango tree and a virus are all living off another living being.
Gut worms take food, but people with no worms at all seem to get more allergies. Scientists are still working out why.
explanations.art: A food web drawn with solid arrows between a leaf, a cricket, a trout and a kingfisher, and thin dotted arrows from small worms to every one of them.

agreed.text: Parasites and their hosts change because of each other, generation after generation.
agreed.evidence: In a New Zealand lake, the commonest families of clone snails were almost completely replaced within 7 to 10 years by families that had been rare. In laboratory tanks, the commonest snail kind went down only when flukes were present.

agreed.text: Some parasites change the proteins on their surface, so that the host's antibodies stop fitting.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have read the genes of sleeping-sickness parasites and found about two thousand coat genes and pieces of genes. In infected animals, a new coat appears in the blood each time the old one is beaten.

agreed.text: Using a medicine selects the parasites who can survive it.
agreed.evidence: Malaria parasites that survive chloroquine were suspected in 1957 and reported in India in 1973. Parasites that artemisinin clears slowly were found in western Cambodia in 2008 and 2009.

agreed.text: Some parasites change what their hosts do, in ways that carry the parasite to the next host.
agreed.evidence: Starlings ate more infected pill bugs than healthy ones when given equal numbers. Birds ate infected killifish 10 to 30 times as often as healthy ones. Mantises with hairworms walked towards the kind of light that water reflects, and healthy mantises did not.

agreed.text: Rabies can be prevented after a bite by washing the wound and giving the vaccine in time.
agreed.evidence: The virus travels slowly along nerves, usually taking two to three months to reach the brain. The World Health Organization reports that washing with soap and water for at least 15 minutes, followed by the vaccine, prevents the disease.

agreed.text: Parasites are a large and ordinary part of the living world.
agreed.evidence: When scientists weighed all the living beings in three river mouths in California and Mexico, the parasites together weighed more than the top hunters, such as the birds.

challenging.claim: Parasites are simple, lazy beings who have lost what other animals have.
challenging.who: Many scientists of the 1800s. Ray Lankester wrote in 1880 that parasites were 'degenerate'.
challenging.for: Many parasites have no eyes, no legs or no gut. A tapeworm soaks up food through the skin.
challenging.against: A parasite gives up what is not needed and builds what is: hooks, coats that change, and ways to pass through three different hosts. A fluke's life needs more separate skills than a snail's.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea of what parasites are like.

challenging.claim: An infected animal behaves oddly only because the animal is ill and weak.
challenging.for: Illness does make animals slow, and many odd behaviours are only that.
challenging.against: Infected pill bugs moved about more than healthy ones, and went to the very places where starlings hunt. Infected rats lost one fear, the fear of cat smell, and kept their other fears.
challenging.context: This card is about why an animal with a parasite may behave strangely.

challenging.claim: The zombie-ant fungus takes over the ant's brain.
challenging.who: Many films, games and news stories
challenging.for: The ant's behaviour changes completely, and behaviour is run by the brain.
challenging.against: When scientists looked inside infected ants in 2017, the fungus was all through the muscles of the body and legs, and they did not find the fungus inside the brain. The fungus may work the muscles directly, or send chemicals to the brain from outside.
challenging.context: This card is about a fungus who grows inside carpenter ants and makes them climb and bite a leaf.

challenging.claim: Toxoplasma, a parasite carried by cats, changes the personality of people.
challenging.who: Jaroslav Flegr and some other researchers
challenging.for: The parasite clearly changes rats. Some studies of people found slower reactions and more road accidents in those infected.
challenging.against: Other large studies found nothing. Infected and uninfected people may differ in food, work and home as well, and those could explain the results.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a common parasite changes how people behave.

challenging.claim: Koel eggs are copies of crow eggs, to fool the crows.
challenging.who: Many bird books, for more than a hundred years
challenging.for: To a human eye, a koel egg and a house crow egg look alike. Egg copying is real in European cuckoos.
challenging.against: A 2021 study in Bangladesh measured the eggs as a bird's eye sees colour, and found no close copying of crows or of two other hosts. Nobody has yet tested how often crows throw out strange eggs.
challenging.context: This card is about the Asian koel, who lays eggs in crows' nests.

challenging.claim: The best plan is to kill every parasite everywhere.
challenging.for: Parasites cause great suffering. Wiping out the Guinea worm and treating children for gut worms have saved many people from pain.
challenging.against: Parasites feed fish and birds, keep any one kind of host from taking over, and are a large share of all living beings. Removing the ones who harm people most is very different from removing them all.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the world would be better with no parasites.

challenging.claim: A dog bite is safe if the dog is a pet or the wound is small.
challenging.for: Most pet dogs who are vaccinated every year do not carry rabies.
challenging.against: Nobody can tell by looking. A scratch or a lick on broken skin can pass the virus, and the disease cannot be cured once it begins. Washing and seeing a doctor the same day costs little.
challenging.context: This card is about what to do after a bite or scratch from a dog, cat or monkey.

big_questions.q: A mantis with a hairworm inside walks into a pond. Who walked: the mantis, the worm, or both?
big_questions.hint: Whose legs moved? Who needed the water? Could one have done it without the other?

big_questions.q: In the Pond Race, no kind of snail stayed the best. Can anything be the best for ever?
big_questions.hint: What made a snail kind do well in one generation? Was that inside the snail, or in who else was in the pond?

big_questions.q: When you sneeze with a cold, the sneeze helps you and helps the virus. Whose sneeze is it?
big_questions.hint: List what the sneeze does for you. List what it does for the virus. Does it have to belong to only one of you?

big_questions.q: A hungry person and a full person choose differently. If something inside you can change what you want, what does 'I chose' mean?
big_questions.hint: Think of times when hunger, tiredness or illness changed what you wanted. Were those choices still yours?

big_questions.q: Parasites cause great suffering. They also keep lakes, forests and bodies in balance. Should people try to remove them all?
big_questions.hint: Think of the Guinea worm, who is almost gone, and of the hairworms who feed trout. Is there one answer for all parasites?

big_questions.q: Hosts and parasites have changed each other for millions of years. Is that a war, or is it a way of living together?
big_questions.hint: In a war, one side hopes to end the other. Does either side in the Pond Race gain if the other disappears?

big_questions.q: How could you find out whether an animal's odd behaviour is a parasite's trick, when you cannot ask the animal?
big_questions.hint: Think of the tests in the Starling Test. What would you compare? What would you count?

story.title: The Mantis Who Walked into the Pond
story.note: Junali, her family and their mantis are made up. These facts are real. Hairworms grow inside praying mantises and crickets, and the adults live in water. Hairworms have been recorded from mantises in India, and most Indian records are from the east and north-east. In many countries people once believed that horse hairs came alive in water, which is why the worms are called horsehair worms. In 2021 a team in Japan showed that mantises with hairworms walk towards light reflected from flat water, and healthy mantises do not. Whether a mantis lives after the worm has left is not well known.
text: The mantis had lived on the hibiscus bush since the month of Jeth, and Junali had watched her nearly every day.

The bush stood by the kitchen wall of the house, in a village a little way from Jorhat in Assam. The mantis was green, and as long as Junali's middle finger. She stood so still among the leaves that Junali's little brother Bhaskar could never find her, even when Junali pointed.

Junali knew three things about her. She ate flies, and held each one in her folded arms like a girl holding a mango. She turned her whole head to look at you, which no other insect did. And she hated water. When the rain came she moved under a leaf. When a drop landed on her she shook it off, one leg at a time.
In the month of Bhado, when the rains were ending, the mantis began to do strange things.

On Monday Junali found her on the lid of the steel water drum by the well. The lid was flat and shone in the sun. The mantis was walking on it in small circles. Junali carried her back to the bush on a stick.
On Wednesday she was on the drum again. On Thursday she was on the tin sheet that covered the firewood. The sheet was wet from the night's rain and shone like a mirror.
'She is looking for something,' Junali said.
'She is looking for flies,' said Bhaskar. 'Flies like the drum.'
But the mantis was not hunting. She was thin in the chest and thick in the belly, and she did not hold her arms ready.

On Friday evening the sun came low under the clouds. The pond behind the house, the pukhuri where the ducks slept, lit up like a brass plate. Junali was shelling peas on the step. She saw the mantis climb down the hibiscus stem to the ground.

A mantis on the ground is a mantis in danger. The hens were not ten steps away. But the mantis did not hide. She walked across the swept yard in a straight line. She walked past the tulsi, past the hens, past the upturned boat. She walked down the bank.
'Bhaskar,' Junali said. 'Come and look.'
The mantis reached the edge of the water. She did not stop. She stepped on to the pond as if it were the steel lid, and then she was in it, with her legs working slowly.
'She is thirsty,' said Bhaskar.
'She has never once gone to water,' said Junali. 'She shakes it off her feet.'
'Then she is stupid.'

Junali broke off a piece of banana leaf and slid it under the mantis. And then she saw the other thing. A dark thread was coming out of the end of the mantis's body. It kept coming. It was as thin as a wire and longer than Junali's forearm. It left the mantis altogether and went winding away through the water, tying and untying itself.
Bhaskar ran for their grandmother.
Aita came down the bank slowly, wiping her hands. She looked at the thread for a long time.
'When I was a girl we called that a horse's hair,' she said. 'People said that if a hair from a horse's tail fell into the water, it came alive.'
'There are no horses here,' said Junali.
'No,' said Aita. 'There never were. I wondered about that, too.'
The mantis lay on the banana leaf. She was alive, but she was flat and light, like an empty pea pod. Junali put her back on the hibiscus, in the fork of two stems.
That night Junali could not sleep. She lay and put the pieces side by side, as she did with sums.
The thread was a worm. The worm had been inside the mantis. That was why the mantis had grown thick in the belly and eaten so much. A worm that long must have been growing there for weeks.
The worm had swum off into the pond as if it were home. Junali had seen threads like that before, in other years, in the shallow end. So the worm was a water animal.
But the mantis was a bush animal. The bush was forty steps from the pond. A worm inside a mantis on a bush has no way to get to a pond. The worm has no legs.
Junali sat up.
The mantis had legs.

She thought of the steel lid, and the wet tin sheet, and the pond at sunset. All three were flat, and all three shone. The mantis had not wanted flies. She had not been thirsty. All week she had been walking towards anything that shone like water. And she had only begun in the week that the worm was full grown.
In the morning she told Bhaskar.
'The mantis did not walk to the pond,' she said. 'The worm did. The worm used her legs.'
'A worm cannot make a mantis walk,' said Bhaskar.
'Then why did she go to the lid on Monday, and the tin on Thursday, and never once before this week? Find me another reason.'
Bhaskar thought about it all through breakfast, and could not.

They went to the hibiscus. The fork of the two stems was empty. Junali looked under every leaf, and Bhaskar looked too, properly this time. They did not find the mantis, and Junali never learned whether she had lived.

But she went on thinking about the walk across the yard. The mantis had gone so straight, and had looked so sure. If you had asked the mantis, Junali thought, she would have said: I want to go to the shining place. And she would have meant it.
story.epiphany: The worm lives in water and has no legs. The mantis lives on a bush and has legs. Junali worked out that the walk to the pond served the worm, and that the mantis had been drawn to anything that shone like water only once the worm was full grown.
ask: Which clues told Junali that the mantis was not simply thirsty?
Why did it matter that the strange walks began only in the last week?
How could you test whether the shine draws the mantis, and not the wetness?
The mantis looked sure of where she was going. Was the wish to reach the shining place her own?
art: A girl of ten in a cotton frock crouching by a hibiscus bush, looking closely at a green praying mantis who has turned her head to look back.
A village pond glowing at sunset, a girl holding a piece of banana leaf under a mantis at the water's edge, and a long dark thread winding away through the water.

games.title: Move and Answer: an arms race card game
games.context: This is a card game about the arms race between hosts and parasites. Each card shows one real move. You guess the other side's answer, which is on the back.

printables.title: 14 move cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: HOST MOVE. People comb and wash their hair.
items.b: PARASITE ANSWER. A louse has claws that lock around one hair, and glues each egg to a hair near the scalp.

items.f: HOST MOVE. The body makes antibodies that grip the coat of a sleeping-sickness parasite.
items.b: PARASITE ANSWER. One parasite switches to a new coat from about two thousand coat genes. The old antibodies no longer fit.

items.f: HOST MOVE. Reed warblers throw out eggs that look unlike their own.
items.b: PARASITE ANSWER. Cuckoos who use reed warbler nests lay eggs that look like reed warbler eggs.

items.f: HOST MOVE. Doctors give chloroquine to cure malaria.
items.b: PARASITE ANSWER. Parasites with a small change in one gene survive. Their young spread. In India this was first reported in Assam in 1973.

items.f: PARASITE MOVE. Malaria parasites become resistant to one medicine.
items.b: HOST ANSWER. Doctors give artemisinin together with a second medicine. A parasite would need the answer to both at once.

items.f: PARASITE MOVE. Flukes come to fit the commonest kind of snail in a lake.
items.b: HOST ANSWER. Snails with two parents have young with new mixes of genes. Many are a rare kind that few flukes fit.

items.f: PARASITE MOVE. A virus injects genes into a bacterium.
items.b: HOST ANSWER. Many bacteria keep a piece of the virus in their own genes. Next time they recognise that virus and cut the virus's genes. This is CRISPR.

items.f: PARASITE MOVE. A tick's saliva numbs the skin, so the bite is not felt.
items.b: HOST ANSWER. Monkeys, cattle and people check and groom each other's skin and hair.

items.f: PARASITE MOVE. The rabies virus travels hidden inside nerves, where antibodies in the blood do not meet the virus.
items.b: HOST ANSWER. People wash the bite and give a vaccine at once. The body is ready before the virus reaches the brain.

items.f: PARASITE MOVE. Hookworm young wait in damp soil and enter through bare skin.
items.b: HOST ANSWER. People wear footwear and build toilets, so that dung with worm eggs stays out of the soil.

items.f: PARASITE MOVE. A female mosquito finds people by the breath they give out and the smell of their skin.
items.b: HOST ANSWER. People sleep under nets, burn coils and put screens on windows.

items.f: PARASITE MOVE. Fungus spores from a dead ant fall on the nest's paths.
items.b: HOST ANSWER. Ants carry dying and dead nest-mates far away from the nest.

items.f: PARASITE MOVE. A malaria parasite puts a marker protein on the outside of the red blood cell they live in.
items.b: HOST ANSWER. The body makes antibodies to the marker. Then the parasite switches to another of about 60 marker genes.

items.f: HOST MOVE. A bird preens every feather with the beak.
items.b: PARASITE ANSWER. Many feather lice are flat and narrow, and slip between the barbs of a feather where the beak cannot reach.

printables.title: A score sheet with a row for each player

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile with the MOVE side up.
On your turn, read the top card aloud. Say what you think the other side's answer is.
Turn the card over and read the back. You get 2 points if your idea matches, even in different words.
Then invent the next move for the side that has just been answered. You get 1 point for any move that could work.
Keep the card. Play until the pile is finished.
With friends, the player with the most points wins. Alone, try to reach 20 points out of 42.
If players disagree about a point, the reader of the card decides.

flow.say: Each card is one real move in a contest between a host and a parasite. Your job is to guess how the other side answered.

ask.q: Did any card end the contest for good?
good: No. Every answer could be answered again.
The comb comes close, because a louse egg cannot quickly become too small for it.

ask.q: Which side changes faster, and why?
good: Usually the parasite. Parasites have new generations in days or weeks.
Medicines and vaccines are fast host moves, because people invent them.

flow.parent: Accept any next move that could really work. For example, after the two-medicine card, a parasite might become resistant to the second medicine first.

flow.do: 1. Add up the points. 2. Lay the cards in two rows, host moves and parasite moves. 3. Ask which answers were made by bodies and which by behaviour.
flow.say: Count your points. Now look at the host answers. Which happen inside a body? Which are things a host does?
flow.kid: Count your points. Sort the host answers. Which are inside a body? Which are things a host does?

check.q: Why is artemisinin always given with a second medicine?
options: A parasite is unlikely to resist both at once
Two medicines taste better together
Parasites cannot change at all
check.why: A parasite would need to be born with the answer to two different medicines at the same time, which is far less likely than one. Picking 'parasites cannot change' misses the whole game: every card shows one side changing in answer to the other.

flow.context: This is the last step of Move and Answer. Here you count your points and sort the host's answers into those inside a body and those that are behaviour.

games.title: How Strong Is the Evidence? A sorting game about parasites who steer their hosts
games.context: This is a card game about how we know things. Each card makes a claim about a parasite who changes a host's behaviour. You decide how strong the evidence is.

printables.title: 13 claim cards to cut out (the verdict is on the back)

items.f: Pill bugs with a certain worm inside walk in the open, and starlings eat more of them.
items.b: TESTED. In 1983 Janice Moore gave starlings equal numbers of infected and healthy pill bugs. The starlings ate more of the infected ones.

items.f: Killifish with a fluke on the brain flash near the surface, and birds eat more of them.
items.b: TESTED. In 1996 birds ate infected fish 10 to 30 times as often in pens in a lagoon. In 2023 fish infected on purpose became more showy.

items.f: Rats with Toxoplasma lose their fear of the smell of cats.
items.b: TESTED. Shown in pens in 2000 and in laboratories in 2007. The rats kept their other fears.

items.f: Rats with Toxoplasma are caught by cats more often outdoors.
items.b: NOT YET TESTED. It fits everything else, but nobody has counted it outdoors.

items.f: Toxoplasma changes the personality of people.
items.b: STILL ARGUED ABOUT. Some studies found small differences. Other large studies found none.

items.f: Mantises with a hairworm inside walk towards the kind of light that water reflects.
items.b: TESTED. In Japan in 2021, infected mantises chose this light in a two-way test. Healthy mantises did not.

items.f: The zombie-ant fungus steers the ant by growing inside the brain.
items.b: STILL ARGUED ABOUT. In 2017 the fungus was found all through the muscles, and was not found inside the brain. How the ant is steered is unknown.

items.f: Ants with the zombie-ant fungus bite a leaf vein at about midday.
items.b: TESTED. Scientists watched and timed infected ants in a forest in Thailand and reported it in 2011.

items.f: Children who carry the mosquito stage of malaria draw more mosquitoes.
items.b: TESTED. In Kenya in 2005 such children drew about twice as many. After medicine, the difference was gone.

items.f: A jewel wasp's sting to the head stops a cockroach from walking off alone.
items.b: TESTED. In 2003 scientists traced the venom to two exact places in the cockroach's brain.

items.f: The burning blister of a Guinea worm makes a person put the foot in water.
items.b: NOT YET TESTED. It has been seen for centuries and it fits. Nobody has compared people in a fair test.

items.f: Rabies makes a dog bite more, and this passes on the virus.
items.b: NOT YET TESTED in a fair comparison. It has been seen for thousands of years, and the virus is in the saliva. Nobody would give dogs rabies to count bites.

items.f: A sneeze is a trick of the cold virus to reach the next person.
items.b: STILL ARGUED ABOUT. A sneeze spreads the virus, and it also clears the nose. It may serve both.

printables.title: A mat with three spaces
items: TESTED: someone compared infected and healthy hosts fairly
NOT YET TESTED: it has been seen and it fits, but nobody has compared
STILL ARGUED ABOUT: the tests disagree, or point both ways

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, claim side up.
On your turn, read the top card aloud. Put it on the space you think is right, and say why.
Turn the card over. If the space is right, keep the card. If not, put it at the bottom of the pile.
Play until every card has been kept.
With friends, the player with the most cards wins. Alone, count how many you get right first time, and try to beat 8.
After the game, choose one NOT YET TESTED card and say how you would test it.
