flow.context: This is the first step of How Strong Is the Evidence? Here you set up the claim cards and the mat with three spaces.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to read the top card. 2. Put it on a space and give a reason. 3. Turn it over and check. 4. Keep it if right, or put it under the pile.
flow.say: Read the claim. Where does it go? Tell me what kind of evidence you would expect before you turn it over.
flow.kid: Read the claim. Choose a space and say why. Turn the card over. Keep it if you were right.

ask.q: Two cards are about rats and Toxoplasma. Why are they on different spaces?
good: Losing the fear of cat smell was tested. Being caught more often outdoors was not.
One is about what the rat does. The other is about what happens next.

ask.q: Why has nobody tested the rabies card fairly?
good: It would mean giving dogs a deadly disease.
Some tests should not be done.

flow.parent: The point is that a good story is not yet evidence. Praise any reason that asks what was compared and what was counted.
flow.context: This is the main part of How Strong Is the Evidence? Here you sort claims about behaviour-changing parasites by how well each has been tested.

flow.do: 1. Count the cards each player kept. 2. Pick one NOT YET TESTED card. 3. Ask how it could be tested without harming anyone.
flow.say: Choose one card that has not been tested. What would you compare? What would you count? Would any animal be harmed?
flow.kid: Count your cards. Pick one untested claim. Say what you would compare and count.

check.q: Infected fish flash more. What else must be shown before calling it a parasite's trick?
options: That birds really eat more infected fish
That the fish are a bright colour
That the fish feel ill
check.why: A change counts as manipulation only if it carries more parasites to the next host. For the killifish, birds ate infected fish 10 to 30 times as often. Picking 'the fish feel ill' mixes up a side effect of illness with a change that helps the parasite.

flow.context: This is the last step of How Strong Is the Evidence? Here you count your cards and plan a fair test for one untested claim.

experiments.title: The Pond Race: does the commonest snail stay on top?
experiments.context: In this experiment, seeds stand for three kinds of snail in a pond, and a card stands for the flukes who infect them. You run the pond for eight generations with a die.
experiments.question: Rajma snails are the commonest kind in the pond at the start. Flukes infect only the kind they fit. After eight generations, which kind of snail is the commonest?
experiments.predict: Guess first. The pond starts with 8 rajma snails, 2 chana snails and 2 moong snails. Which kind will be the commonest after eight generations? Write your guess and why you think so. Then guess for a second pond where all 12 snails are rajma: will it do better or worse, and why?
experiments.fair_test: Both ponds have 12 snails at the start, the same die, the same fluke card and the same rules. Only one thing differs. Pond 1 has three kinds of snail and pond 2 has one kind.

materials.item: rajma (red kidney beans)
kabuli chana (white chickpeas)
whole green moong, or any third seed that looks different
a die
a steel tumbler and a small plate
paper, a pencil and an eraser

schedule.what: Set up a pond of 12 seed snails and a fluke card. Run eight generations with a die. Then run a second pond of 12 rajma snails and compare.

experiments.record: Fill in one row of the table for each generation of pond 1. Make a second table for pond 2. Then draw a line graph for pond 1, with the generation along the bottom and the number of snails up the side. Use one coloured line for each kind of snail.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results from one pond 1
rows: R R C C M M
R R R R C M
R R R R C M
R R R R C M
R C C C C M
R C C C C M
R C C C C M
R C C C C M
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a filled table can look like. Your pond will be different, because the die decides.

setup.art: Twelve seeds in a row on a table, eight red rajma, two pale chana and two green moong, with three small heaps of spare seeds behind them.
setup.caption: 1. Count out 8 rajma, 2 chana and 2 moong. These are the 12 snails.

setup.art: A strip of paper with six boxes numbered 1 to 6, holding the letters R, R, C, C, M, M in pencil, and a die beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the fluke card. Boxes 1 and 2 are R, 3 and 4 are C, 5 and 6 are M.

setup.art: A child rolling a die beside a rajma seed, with a finger on box 2 of the card, and a small plate holding two seeds labelled infected.
setup.caption: 3. Roll for each snail. If the box matches the snail, she is infected.

setup.art: A steel tumbler with seeds inside, a hand taking seeds out with eyes closed, and a table of numbers being filled in.
setup.caption: 4. Healthy snails each have a baby. Shake, take out 12, and change the card.

flow.do: 1. Count out 8 rajma, 2 chana and 2 moong for pond 1. 2. Put the spare seeds in three heaps. This is the store. 3. Draw six boxes in a row and number them 1 to 6. 4. In pencil, write R in boxes 1 and 2, C in 3 and 4, M in 5 and 6. 5. Draw the results table. 6. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write both down.
flow.say: Each seed is a snail. Rajma snails are the commonest kind. The card shows the flukes, and a fluke can infect only the snail with her letter. Which snail will be commonest after eight generations? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Count out 8 rajma, 2 chana and 2 moong. Draw the card with six boxes. Write R, R, C, C, M, M. Now guess. Which snail will be commonest after eight generations? Write why.
flow.parent: Many children guess rajma, because rajma starts far ahead. Others guess that all three will end equal. Write the guess and the reason down without comment. The pond will answer.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Pond Race. Here you set up 12 seed snails and a fluke card, and guess which kind of snail will be commonest after eight generations.

flow.do: 1. Lay the 12 snails in a row. 2. Roll the die for the first snail and look at that box on the card. 3. If the letter matches the snail, she is infected. Move her to the plate. 4. Do this for every snail. Write how many of each kind were infected. 5. Give each healthy snail one baby of her own kind from the store. 6. Put the healthy snails and the babies in the tumbler and shake. 7. Without looking, take out 12. If there are fewer than 12, use them all. 8. If a kind is missing, swap one seed of the commonest kind for the missing kind. 9. Change the card. The fluke who infected the most snails gets boxes 1 to 4. The other two get boxes 5 and 6. If there is a tie for most, leave the card alone. 10. Put all other seeds back in the store. Write the new counts. Do generations 2, 3 and 4.
flow.say: An infected snail has no babies, so she leaves the pond. Each healthy snail has one baby. The fluke who found the most snails has the most young, so she fills four boxes. Tell me what you see happening.
flow.kid: Roll for each snail. If the box matches her, she is infected. Put infected snails on the plate. Each healthy snail gets one baby. Shake them and take out 12. If a kind is missing, swap one in. The fluke with most snails gets boxes 1 to 4. The others get boxes 5 and 6. A tie means no change. Write the counts. Do four generations.

ask.q: Which snail kind was infected most in generation 2? Why that kind?
good: Usually rajma. After generation 1 the card often has R in four boxes.
The commonest snail gave the most hosts to her fluke.

flow.parent: One generation takes about 3 minutes once the rules are clear. Step 8 stands for a snail of the missing kind drifting in from the next pond. If your child feels for a favourite seed in the tumbler, tip out 12 instead.
flow.context: In this step of the Pond Race you run the first four generations. A die decides which seed snails are infected, and the fluke card changes after each generation.

flow.do: 1. Run generations 5 to 8 by the same rules. 2. After each one, circle the commonest snail kind in the table. 3. After generation 8, compare the result with the guess.
flow.say: Keep going to generation 8. Each time, circle the commonest snail. Now look down the table. What happened to the commonest kind? What did the card do each time?
flow.kid: Run generations 5 to 8. Circle the commonest snail each time. Look down your table. What happened to the commonest kind?

ask.q: What happened to the kind that was commonest?
good: The commonest kind was infected most and went down.
A kind that was rare took over, and then the card turned to that kind.

ask.q: Was any kind of snail the best all the way through?
good: No. The lead changed.
Each kind was safest when rare.

flow.parent: In most ponds the commonest kind changes at least once in eight generations, and rajma ends on top in about one pond in ten. If rajma led all the way, that is a real result. Write it down and run four more generations.
flow.context: In this step of the Pond Race you run generations 5 to 8 and look at what happened to the commonest kind of seed snail.

flow.do: 1. Clear the table. Count out 12 rajma for pond 2. 2. Rub out the card and write R, R, C, C, M, M again. 3. Ask whether pond 2 will do better or worse than pond 1, and why. 4. Run pond 2 by the same rules for up to eight generations. 5. Stop early if no healthy snail is left. 6. Write the number of snails after each generation.
flow.say: In this pond every snail is a rajma snail. They are all copies of one mother. Will this pond do better or worse than the first? Why? Now run it and count the snails each time.
flow.kid: Make pond 2 with 12 rajma. Reset the card. Guess: better or worse than pond 1? Say why. Run it by the same rules. Count the snails each time.

ask.q: What did the fluke card do in pond 2?
good: The rajma fluke took four boxes and kept them.
There was no other kind for the flukes to turn to, and no rare snail to escape.

flow.parent: Pond 2 usually shrinks to 4 snails or fewer by generation 8, and is often empty by generation 6 or 7. About one time in twenty the die is kind and the pond lasts. Then run four more generations.
flow.context: In this step of the Pond Race you run a second pond in which all 12 seed snails are of one kind, and compare it with the mixed pond.

flow.do: 1. Draw the line graph for pond 1, with one coloured line for each snail kind. 2. Mark where the lines cross. 3. Ask for three sentences: what I thought, what I saw, and why it happened.
flow.say: Draw one line for each kind of snail. Where do the lines cross? Now tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Draw one line for each snail kind. Mark where the lines cross. Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

check.q: A pond has 10 chana snails, 1 rajma snail and 1 moong snail. Which fluke will do best in the next few generations?
options: The chana fluke
The rajma fluke
All three equally
check.why: The chana fluke meets a snail she fits ten times out of twelve, so she has the most young and fills the card. Then chana snails are infected most and go down. Picking 'all three equally' usually means thinking of flukes as fixed. The flukes change with the snails.

flow.parent: A strong answer says that being common made a snail kind the main target, and that the mixed pond lasted because some kind was always rare. Only after your child has said this, read the explanation card on why the commonest kind does not stay on top.
flow.think: In pond 1, was any kind of snail the best? What would 'best' mean?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Pond Race. Here you draw a line graph of the three kinds of seed snail and say what the two ponds showed.

experiments.title: The Starling Test: how much does a small change in behaviour matter?
experiments.context: In this experiment paper circles stand for pill bugs, and a person plays a hungry starling. Some bugs carry a hidden dot, which stands for a worm inside. You test whether the dot, or the place where the bug stands, decides who is caught.
experiments.question: Pill bugs with a worm inside walk in the open. If 10 bugs stand in the open and 10 hide, how many times as many of the open ones does a hunter catch? And does the worm alone, with no change in behaviour, make any difference?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Ten paper bugs lie in the open on pale paper and ten hide among leaves on a dark cloth. In 10 seconds, how many of each will the hunter catch? Then guess what happens when all twenty hide in the same way. Write both guesses and why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Every round has 20 bugs of the same size and colour, the same hunter, one hand and 10 seconds. Only the place of the 10 dotted bugs changes: in the open, on the dark cloth without cover, or hidden like the others.

materials.item: dark paper, such as a brown paper bag or black chart paper
a dark cloth, such as a towel, a bedsheet or a dupatta
white paper or newspaper
dry leaves, or crumpled pieces of the same dark paper
a cup, a pencil and scissors

experiments.safety: A grown-up helps with the scissors.

schedule.what: Cut 20 paper bugs and dot 10 of them underneath. Hunt them for 10 seconds in three different set-ups, twice each. Compare how many dotted and plain bugs are caught.

experiments.record: Fill in one row of the table for each of the six rounds. Add up the dotted bugs and the plain bugs caught in each set-up. Draw a bar chart with two bars for each set-up.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: bugs caught in two rounds of 10 seconds
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: Twenty small dark paper circles on a table, ten of them turned over to show a pencil dot, with scissors and a one-rupee coin for size.
setup.caption: 1. Cut 20 dark paper bugs the size of a one-rupee coin. Dot 10 underneath.

setup.art: A dark towel on the floor with dry leaves on it and plain paper bugs half hidden among the leaves, and beside it white paper with ten paper bugs lying in the open.
setup.caption: 2. Hide the 10 plain bugs among leaves on the dark cloth. Put the 10 dotted bugs on the white paper.

setup.art: A child picking up paper bugs one at a time with one hand and dropping them in a cup, while another child counts aloud.
setup.caption: 3. The hunter has 10 seconds and one hand. One bug at a time goes in the cup.

setup.art: The same dark towel with all twenty bugs hidden among the leaves and the white paper taken away.
setup.caption: 4. Last, hide all 20 in the same way and hunt again.

flow.do: 1. Cut 20 circles of dark paper, each the size of a one-rupee coin. 2. Put a pencil dot on one side of 10 of them. 3. Spread the dark cloth on the floor and scatter the leaves on it. 4. Lay the white paper beside the cloth. 5. Draw the results table. 6. Ask for the guesses and the reasons.
flow.say: Each circle is a pill bug. A dot underneath means a worm inside. Healthy bugs hide. Bugs with a worm walk in the open. How many of each will a hunter catch in 10 seconds? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to help you cut 20 dark circles. Dot 10 underneath. Spread the cloth and the leaves. Now guess. How many of each kind will be caught? Write why.
flow.parent: Keep the dots small and underneath, so that the hunter cannot tell the bugs apart from above. Write the guesses down. Many children expect only a small difference.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Starling Test. Here you make 20 paper pill bugs, mark 10 with a hidden dot, and guess how many of each a hunter will catch.

flow.do: 1. The hunter turns away. 2. Hide the 10 plain bugs among the leaves on the dark cloth. 3. Put the 10 dotted bugs on the white paper, dot side down. 4. Say go and count slowly to 10. 5. The hunter picks up one bug at a time with one hand and drops each in the cup. 6. Count the dotted and plain bugs in the cup. Write them down. 7. Do the round once more.
flow.say: You are a starling with ten seconds to feed. Use one hand, and take one bug at a time. Go. Now turn them over. How many have a dot?
flow.kid: Hunter, turn away. Setter, hide the plain bugs and put the dotted bugs in the open. Hunt for 10 seconds with one hand. Count dotted and plain bugs. Do it twice. Working alone? Set the bugs, leave the room, count to 30, then hunt.

ask.q: How many times as many dotted bugs as plain bugs did you catch?
good: Any number worked out from the counts, such as 15 and 4, which is nearly 4 times.
Many more dotted ones, because they were easy to see and reach.

flow.parent: Expect most of the open bugs to be caught and only a few hidden ones. If the hunter catches every bug in 10 seconds, cut the time to 6 seconds for all rounds.
flow.context: In this step of the Starling Test the dotted paper bugs stand in the open and the plain ones hide. A hunter has 10 seconds to catch as many as possible.

flow.do: 1. Take the white paper away. 2. Put the 10 dotted bugs on the dark cloth, in the gaps between the leaves and not under them. 3. Hide the 10 plain bugs among the leaves as before. 4. Hunt for 10 seconds. Count and write. 5. Do the round once more.
flow.say: Now the dotted bugs are on the dark cloth, but they are not under the leaves. This is a smaller change in behaviour. Will it still matter? Go.
flow.kid: Take away the white paper. Put the dotted bugs on the cloth, between the leaves. Hide the plain bugs. Hunt for 10 seconds. Count. Do it twice.

ask.q: Was a small change in behaviour enough to change who was caught?
good: Yes, the dotted bugs were still caught more often, but by less.
It depended. Dark bugs on a dark cloth were harder to see.

flow.parent: Results vary here, and that is fine. Dark bugs on a dark cloth are harder to see, so the gap usually shrinks. Write down what you get.
flow.context: In this step of the Starling Test the dotted paper bugs stand on the dark cloth but outside the cover of the leaves. You test whether a smaller change in behaviour still matters.

flow.do: 1. Mix all 20 bugs. 2. Hide all of them among the leaves on the dark cloth in the same way. 3. Hunt for 10 seconds. Count dotted and plain. 4. Do the round once more.
flow.say: This is the control. Now the dotted bugs behave exactly like the others. If the worm alone made a bug easy to catch, what would we see? Go.
flow.kid: Mix all the bugs. Hide them all in the same way. Hunt for 10 seconds. Count dotted and plain. Do it twice.

ask.q: Were dotted bugs caught more often when they hid like the others?
good: No. About the same number of each was caught.
The dot made no difference. The place did.

flow.parent: Expect about equal numbers, give or take one or two. This round shows that the difference in the first rounds came from where the bugs stood.
flow.context: In this step of the Starling Test all 20 paper bugs hide in the same way. This is the control round, where the dotted bugs behave like the plain ones.

flow.do: 1. Add up the two rounds for each set-up. 2. Draw the bar chart. 3. Ask for three sentences: what I thought, what I saw, and why it happened. 4. Then read the true story of Janice Moore's pill bugs on the card How we found out.
flow.say: Look at the three set-ups. When were dotted bugs caught most? When were they caught no more than the others? What did you think, what did you see, and why did it happen?
flow.kid: Add up each set-up. Draw the bars. Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

check.q: In the control round, dotted and plain bugs were caught equally. What does that show?
options: Where a bug stands decides who is caught
The hunter was tired by then
Dotted bugs are slower
check.why: When the dotted bugs hid like the others, the dot made no difference. So the earlier difference came from their place, which stands for their behaviour. Picking 'dotted bugs are slower' is the old idea that infected animals are simply weak. Paper bugs cannot be slow, and Janice Moore's real infected pill bugs moved more, not less.

flow.parent: This is a model. Real pill bugs with the worm were also found on paler ground and in drier air, and real starlings did eat more of them. Paper cannot show whether a real infected bug is weaker, which Janice Moore checked separately.
flow.think: The worm cannot see a starling. So how can a worm's host end up where starlings hunt?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Starling Test. Here you compare the three set-ups and say whether the dot or the place decided which paper bugs were caught.

activities.title: Who Gains? Sort eight strange behaviours
activities.context: In this activity you hear eight true things that animals do. For each one, you decide who gains from it: the animal, a parasite inside the animal, or nobody.

materials.item: a notebook page and a pencil

schedule.what: Hear eight true animal behaviours. Sort each by who gains. Then learn what is inside each animal and sort again.

activities.record: Draw a table with four columns: the behaviour, my first guess of who gains, what is inside the animal, and my second answer.

setup.art: A notebook page with a four-column table and the first row filled in with the words mantis walks into pond.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a table with four columns.

setup.art: A parent reading from a phone while a child writes a guess in the second column.
setup.caption: 2. Hear each behaviour. Write who you think gains.

setup.art: The same table with the third column filled in with words such as hairworm, virus and nothing, and some guesses crossed out and changed.
setup.caption: 3. Learn what is inside each animal. Answer again.

flow.do: 1. Read the eight behaviours aloud, one at a time. 2. After each, ask who gains from it, and why. 3. Your child writes a guess. Do not say what is inside the animal yet.
flow.say: Here are eight true things. One, a mantis walks into a pond. Two, a lizard sits in the hot sun for much longer than usual. Three, a crow pulls every feather through the beak. Four, a rat walks towards the smell of a cat. Five, a person sneezes hard. Six, a goat lies down all day and eats little. Seven, an ant climbs a plant and bites a leaf at midday. Eight, a dog bites at anything that moves. For each, who gains?
flow.kid: Read the eight behaviours in the list. For each, write who gains. Is it the animal, someone else, or nobody? Say why.
flow.parent: Listen to the reasons. Most children say the animal gains from every one, or that some are just silly. Both guesses are a good place to start.
flow.context: This is the first step of Who Gains? Here you hear eight true animal behaviours and guess who gains from each.

flow.do: 1. Now read what is inside each animal. 2. Ask your child to answer again for each. 3. Ask what changed their mind.
flow.say: Now the hidden part. The mantis has a hairworm, who must reach water. The lizard has an infection, and heat slows the microbes. The crow has feather lice. The rat has a parasite who can mate only in a cat. The person has a cold virus. The goat has many gut worms. The ant has a fungus, whose spores must fall on the path. The dog has the rabies virus in the saliva. Who gains now?
flow.kid: Now read what is inside each animal. Answer again for each one. Which answers did you change? Why?

ask.q: Which behaviours help the animal who does them?
good: The lizard in the sun and the crow preening.
They are defences against parasites.

ask.q: Which one could help both sides?
good: The sneeze. It clears the nose and it spreads the virus.

flow.parent: The mantis, rat, ant and dog serve the parasite. The lizard and crow serve themselves. The sneeze may serve both. The goat may only be weak, which is a side effect, and nobody is sure.
flow.context: In this step of Who Gains? you learn which parasite or microbe is inside each of the eight animals, and decide again who gains from each behaviour.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to pick the behaviour they are least sure of. 2. Ask how someone could find out who gains.
flow.say: Which one are you least sure about? How could a scientist find out who gains from it? What would she compare?
flow.kid: Pick the one you are least sure about. How could someone find out who gains?

check.q: A lizard with an infection sits longer in the sun. Who gains?
options: The lizard, because heat slows the microbes
The microbes, because they like heat
Nobody gains
check.why: A hotter body slows many microbes, so basking is the lizard's own defence, like a fever. Picking 'the microbes' usually means thinking that every odd behaviour of an ill animal is the parasite's doing. Some are the host fighting back.

flow.context: This is the last step of Who Gains? Here you choose the behaviour you are least sure about and say how its gain could be tested.

activities.title: The Coat Change: draw the waves of a long infection
activities.context: In this activity you follow a made-up parasite who doubles every day and changes coat. You draw a graph of the number of parasites, day by day, and see why the illness comes in waves.

materials.item: squared paper, or a notebook page and a ruler
coloured pencils

schedule.what: Work out the number of parasites each day for 13 days, first with one coat and then with coat changing. Draw both as line graphs.

activities.record: Make a table with a row for each day from 1 to 13, and columns for coat A, coat B, coat C, coat D and the total. Then draw a line graph of the total, with the day along the bottom.

example_chart.title: The model's totals for a parasite who changes coat
example_chart.note: These numbers come from the rules of this model. Real infections have millions of parasites, and their waves are less even.

setup.art: A notebook table with days 1 to 13 down the side and the columns Coat A, Coat B, Coat C, Coat D and Total, with the first five rows of Coat A filled in as 1, 2, 4, 8, 16.
setup.caption: 1. Coat A starts with 1 parasite and doubles each day for 5 days.

setup.art: The same table with a zero in Coat A on day 6 and Coat B starting with a 1 on day 5.
setup.caption: 2. On day 6 the body has learned coat A. One parasite had already switched to coat B.

setup.art: A line graph on squared paper with three sharp peaks of equal height.
setup.caption: 3. Add up each day and draw the line.

flow.do: 1. Read the three rules of the model aloud. 2. Fill in coat A for days 1 to 6 together. 3. Ask what the graph would look like if the parasite had only one coat.
flow.say: Rule one: a coat starts with 1 parasite and doubles every day. Rule two: the body needs 5 days to learn a coat. On the sixth day, every parasite in that coat is gone. Fill in coat A. What happens on day 6?
flow.kid: A coat starts with 1 parasite. It doubles each day. On its sixth day the body wipes it out. Fill in coat A for six days.

ask.q: With only one coat, how long does the infection last?
good: Five days. On day 6 the body has learned the coat and all the parasites are gone.

flow.parent: Coat A reads 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and then 0. These numbers are made up to keep the sums small. In a real body the first antibodies take one to two weeks.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Coat Change. Here you learn the rules of a made-up parasite and work out what happens when the parasite has only one coat.

flow.do: 1. Read rule three. 2. Start coat B with 1 parasite on day 5, and double it for 5 days. 3. Start coat C on day 9 and coat D on day 13. 4. Add up the total for each day.
flow.say: Rule three: on the day a coat reaches 8 parasites, one of them switches. The next day there is 1 parasite in a new coat. The body has to start learning again. Fill in coats B, C and D, and add up each day.
flow.kid: When a coat reaches 8, one parasite switches. The next day a new coat starts with 1. Fill in coats B, C and D. Add up each day.

ask.q: What is the total on day 5, and why is it not 16?
good: 17. There are 16 in coat A and 1 in the new coat B.

flow.parent: The totals are 1, 2, 4, 8, 17, 2, 4, 8, 17, 2, 4, 8, 17. Coat A is gone on day 6, when coat B has 2.
flow.context: In this step of the Coat Change you add a rule that lets one made-up parasite switch to a new coat, and work out the number of parasites for 13 days.

flow.do: 1. Draw the line graph of the totals. 2. Ask what shape it makes. 3. Ask how long the infection could last if the parasite had 2,000 coats.
flow.say: Draw the line. What shape do you see? The real sleeping-sickness parasite has about two thousand coat genes. What does that tell you about how long the illness can last?
flow.kid: Draw the line graph. What shape is it? The real parasite has about 2,000 coats. How long could the illness go on?

check.q: In this model, why does the number of parasites fall every few days?
options: The body has learned that coat
The parasites get tired
The medicine has worked
check.why: Each fall comes when antibodies for one coat are ready and clear every parasite wearing it. The number rises again because one parasite had already switched to a coat the body has not met. Picking 'the medicine has worked' adds something that is not in the model. No medicine was given.

flow.parent: The graph is a row of equal waves. In the model a new coat appears every 4 days, so 2,000 coats would last 8,000 days, about 22 years. Real switching is less tidy, and many coat genes are broken pieces that the parasite joins together.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Coat Change. Here you draw the graph of a made-up parasite who keeps switching coats, and say why the line goes up and down in waves.

activities.title: The Preening Count: how much of a bird's time goes to fighting parasites?
activities.context: In this activity you watch a crow, a pigeon or a myna from a window or balcony. You count how often the bird is preening, which is one way a host fights lice and mites.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a clock or phone that shows seconds

schedule.what: Watch one resting bird for 10 minutes and mark what the bird is doing every 30 seconds. Repeat with a second bird. Work out the fraction of looks spent preening.

activities.record: Draw two rows of 20 boxes, one row for each bird. In each box write P for preening or scratching, or N for anything else. Under each row write the fraction of boxes with P.

setup.art: A child at a balcony railing with a notebook, looking at a crow perched on a wire across the lane.
setup.caption: 1. Find a bird who is resting on a wire, a ledge or a branch.

setup.art: A notebook page with a row of 20 small boxes, some holding the letter P and some the letter N, and a phone showing a timer.
setup.caption: 2. Every 30 seconds, look up and write P or N.

setup.art: A close view of a crow drawing one wing feather through the beak.
setup.caption: 3. P means preening: running a feather through the beak, or scratching.

flow.do: 1. Go to a window or balcony. 2. Find a crow, pigeon, myna or sparrow who is resting, not feeding. 3. Draw two rows of 20 boxes. 4. Ask for a guess: out of 20 looks, how many will show preening?
flow.say: Preening means pulling a feather through the beak, or scratching with a foot. Out of 20 looks, how many times do you think this bird will be preening? Why?
flow.kid: Find a resting bird. Draw two rows of 20 boxes. Guess how many of 20 looks will show preening. Write why.
flow.parent: Mid-morning and late afternoon are good times, when birds rest between feeds. If no bird is in view, watch a street dog, a cat or a cow from a distance and count scratching, licking and tail swishing.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Preening Count. Here you find a resting bird and guess how often the bird will be preening.

flow.do: 1. Start the timer. 2. Every 30 seconds, look at the bird and write P or N in the next box. 3. Stop after 20 boxes. 4. If the bird flies off, carry on with another bird of the same kind. 5. Fill a second row for a different bird if there is time.
flow.say: Look only when the 30 seconds are up. Write what the bird is doing at that moment. That keeps the count fair.
flow.kid: Every 30 seconds, look up. Write P for preening or N for not. Fill 20 boxes. Then do a second bird.

ask.q: Why do we look only every 30 seconds, and not whenever the bird does something?
good: So that we do not count only the times that catch our eye.
It makes each look count the same.

flow.parent: Resting birds often preen in several of the 20 looks, but this varies a lot with the bird, the weather and the time of day. Any result is worth writing down.
flow.context: In this step of the Preening Count you look at a resting bird every 30 seconds and write whether the bird is preening.

flow.do: 1. Count the boxes with P in each row. 2. Write each as a fraction of 20. 3. Ask what the bird gives up to preen, and what would happen if the bird stopped.
flow.say: How many of the 20 looks showed preening? Write it as a fraction. What could the bird have been doing with that time? So why preen?
flow.kid: Count the P boxes. Write the fraction out of 20. What does the bird give up to preen? Why do it?

check.q: Preening costs a bird time. Why do birds still preen so much?
options: Lice and mites would multiply and damage the feathers
Birds enjoy looking tidy for people
Preening has no use
check.why: Lice and mites feed on feathers and skin. Preening removes many of them and also keeps the feathers in order for flying. A defence that costs this much time shows how much parasites matter to a host. Picking 'no use' misses that birds who cannot preen properly carry far more lice.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Preening Count. Here you work out what fraction of the looks showed preening, and think about why a bird spends time on it.

activities.title: The Fifteen-Minute Wash: practise the dog-bite steps
activities.context: In this activity you practise what to do after a bite or scratch from a dog, a cat or a monkey. Rabies is prevented by doing four steps at once, and the first one takes longer than people think.

materials.item: soap, a bucket of water and a mug, or a tap
a clock or phone timer
a card or half a sheet of paper, and a pen

schedule.what: Time an ordinary hand wash. Then wash a pretend bite for 3 full minutes and work out how long 15 minutes is. Make a steps card for the wall.

activities.record: Write a card with the four steps and keep it where the family can see it: wash for 15 minutes with soap and running water, tell a grown-up at once, see a doctor the same day, take every dose of the vaccine.

setup.art: A child washing a spot on the forearm with soap under water poured from a mug, while a phone timer stands on the bathroom shelf.
setup.caption: 1. Wash a pretend bite with soap and running water. Time it.

setup.art: A child telling her father something while pointing at her leg, and the father kneeling to look.
setup.caption: 2. Practise saying it: a dog scratched me.

setup.art: A hand-written card stuck on a fridge door with four numbered steps and small drawings of a tap, a parent, a doctor and a calendar.
setup.caption: 3. Write the four steps on a card for the wall.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to wash their hands as they usually do. Time it without saying so. 2. Tell them the time. 3. Ask how long a bite should be washed.
flow.say: That wash took this many seconds. Now think of a bite from a dog. How long do you think a doctor would want you to wash it? Why?
flow.kid: Wash your hands as usual. Ask someone to time you. Now guess. How long should a dog bite be washed?
flow.parent: An ordinary wash is often 10 to 20 seconds. Most children guess one minute at most for a bite.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Fifteen-Minute Wash. Here you time an ordinary hand wash and guess how long a bite should be washed.

flow.do: 1. Mark a pretend bite on the forearm with a pen dot. 2. Start the timer. 3. Your child soaps the place and rinses it under running or poured water, again and again, for 3 minutes. 4. Stop. Say that the real wash is five times as long.
flow.say: The World Health Organization says at least 15 minutes, with soap and running water. We will do 3 minutes now. Keep soaping and rinsing. The soap breaks up the virus, and the water carries the virus away.
flow.kid: Mark a dot on your arm. Soap it and rinse it for 3 minutes. Do not stop early. The real wash is 15 minutes. That is five times as long.

ask.q: Why does washing help against a virus in a wound?
good: The virus is in the saliva left in the wound.
Soap breaks the virus up, and water carries the virus away from the nerves.

flow.parent: Use a mug and bucket if water is short. Three minutes feels long, and that is the lesson. Say clearly that a real bite gets the full 15 minutes, and then a doctor.
flow.context: In this step of the Fifteen-Minute Wash you wash a pretend bite with soap and running water for 3 minutes, and work out how long the real 15 minutes is.

flow.do: 1. Practise the telling. Your child says: 'A dog scratched me.' You answer: 'Thank you for telling me. Let us wash it.' 2. Write the four steps on a card together. 3. Add what not to do: no chilli, oil or turmeric on the wound. 4. Stick the card up.
flow.say: Many children hide a bite because they fear a scolding. I promise I will never scold you for telling me. Now tell me the four steps in order.
flow.kid: Practise saying: a dog scratched me. Write the four steps on a card. Wash for 15 minutes. Tell a grown-up. See a doctor today. Take every dose.

check.q: A puppy scratches your leg and it bleeds only a little. What do you do first?
options: Wash with soap and water for 15 minutes
Wait and see if it hurts tomorrow
Put turmeric on it and tell nobody
check.why: Washing at once removes much of the virus, and then a grown-up and a doctor decide about the vaccine. A small scratch from a puppy can still pass rabies. Picking 'wait and see' is the dangerous choice, because once signs of rabies begin there is no cure.

flow.parent: Also agree on two habits. Do not touch or tease dogs you do not know, and do not touch an animal who is ill or dead. A pet dog needs a rabies vaccine every year.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Fifteen-Minute Wash. Here you practise telling a grown-up about a bite and write the four steps on a card.

projects.title: Case File: one parasite who steers a host
projects.context: In this four-day project you choose one parasite who changes a host's behaviour. You make a one-page case file on the evidence, and your family decides whether the case is proved.

materials.item: a large sheet of paper or four notebook pages
a pencil and coloured pencils
the cards of the game How Strong Is the Evidence?

schedule.what: Choose a parasite. Draw the host, the parasite and the place the parasite needs to reach.
Write the evidence: what was compared and what was counted.
Write what is still unknown, and plan one test of your own.
Present the case to your family. They vote: trick, defence, side effect or not proved.

projects.record: Your case file has five parts on one page: the host and the parasite, what changes, the evidence, what nobody knows yet, and my own test.

setup.art: A large sheet of paper divided into five boxes with headings, and a drawing of a mantis and a long thin worm in the first box.
setup.caption: 1. Choose one parasite and draw the host and the journey.

setup.art: A child copying facts from a small claim card into the box headed Evidence.
setup.caption: 2. Write what scientists compared and counted.

setup.art: A child holding up the finished sheet in front of three family members sitting on a sofa, one of whom has a hand raised.
setup.caption: 3. Present the case. The family votes.

flow.do: 1. Read out the choices: hairworm and mantis, fungus and ant, Toxoplasma and rat, fluke and killifish, jewel wasp and cockroach, rabies virus and dog. 2. Your child picks one. 3. They draw the host, the parasite and where the parasite must get to next.
flow.say: Pick the one that puzzles you most. Draw the host and the parasite. Where does the parasite need to go next? Can the parasite get there alone?
flow.kid: Pick one parasite from the list. Draw the host and the parasite. Draw where the parasite must go next.

ask.q: Why can the parasite not get there alone?
good: A hairworm has no legs and cannot cross dry ground.
A fluke in a fish can reach a bird only if the bird eats the fish.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Case File project. Here you choose one behaviour-changing parasite and draw the host, the parasite and the place the parasite must reach.

flow.do: 1. Find your parasite in the explanation cards and the evidence game. 2. Write what scientists compared. 3. Write what they counted and what they found. 4. Watch one of the unit's videos if it shows your parasite.
flow.say: A case needs evidence. What did the scientists compare? What did they count? What did they find?
flow.kid: Find your parasite in the cards. Write what was compared. Write what was counted. Write what was found.
flow.parent: For rabies and the Guinea worm, the honest answer is that no fair comparison has been made. That is worth writing in the file.
flow.context: In this step of the Case File project you write down the evidence for your chosen parasite: what scientists compared and what they counted.

flow.do: 1. Ask what is still not known about this parasite. 2. Your child writes it down. 3. They plan one test that would harm no animal. 4. They say what result would change their mind.
flow.say: What does nobody know yet about your parasite? Plan one test of your own. It must not hurt any animal. What result would make you change your mind?
flow.kid: Write what nobody knows yet. Plan one test that hurts no animal. Say what result would change your mind.

ask.q: What would you compare in your test?
good: Infected hosts with healthy hosts, in the same place and at the same time.

flow.context: In this step of the Case File project you write what is still unknown about your chosen parasite and plan a test of your own.

flow.do: 1. Your child presents the five parts of the case file to the family. 2. Each listener asks one question. 3. Everyone votes: trick, defence, side effect or not proved. 4. Your child writes the vote on the file.
flow.say: Present your case. We will each ask one question. Then we vote. Is this a parasite's trick, the host's defence, a side effect, or not proved?
flow.kid: Present your case file. Answer one question from each person. Ask everyone to vote. Write the vote down.

check.q: Which evidence best shows that a behaviour change is a parasite's trick?
options: More infected hosts reach the parasite's next home
The infected host looks strange
The story is told in many films
check.why: The change must carry more parasites onward, as when birds ate more infected killifish. Looking strange could be a side effect of illness. Picking 'many films' mixes up how often a story is told with how well it has been tested.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Case File project. Here you present your case file to your family and they vote on whether the parasite's trick is proved.

challenges.title: The Mixed Field: plant 36 plots so that one disease cannot take them all
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about variety. You plan a banana field with three varieties, and test your plan against a disease that spreads only through plots of one variety.
challenges.problem: Lakshmi grows bananas near Tiruchirappalli. Her field has 36 plots, in 6 rows of 6. She grows 12 plots each of three varieties: Poovan, Rasthali and Nendran. A fungus in the soil fits one variety at a time. It starts in one plot and spreads to every plot of the same variety that touches it side to side, and then onward from those. Plan where to plant each variety so that an outbreak takes as few plots as possible.
constraints: Use exactly 12 plots of each variety.
Every plot must touch at least one plot of its own variety, side to side, so that Lakshmi can walk through each variety at harvest.
Plots that touch only at a corner do not count as touching.
Test your plan with five outbreaks and work out the average loss.
general: Three big blocks of 12 plots are the easiest to plant and harvest. One outbreak takes a whole block of 12.
Rows of one variety, in the order Poovan, Rasthali, Nendran and again, lose 6 plots in an outbreak.
Smaller groups lose less. The smallest group the rules allow is 2 plots.
creative: Plant pairs of plots, and colour the pairs so that no two pairs of the same variety touch side to side. Then any outbreak takes only 2 plots.
Change which variety grows in which plot every few years, so that the fungus in the soil of a plot meets a new variety.
Keep a few plants of older, rarer varieties in a corner. If a new fungus beats all three main ones, a rare one may survive.
Farmers in several villages can each grow a different mix, so that the whole district is one large mixed field.
challenges.your_turn: Now draw your own 6 by 6 field and colour it. For each outbreak, roll the die twice to choose a row and a column. Shade that plot and every plot of the same variety joined to it side to side. Count the plots lost. Do five outbreaks, starting fresh each time, and work out the average. Then try to beat your own plan.

setup.art: A 6 by 6 grid on squared paper coloured in three large blocks of yellow, green and orange, with one block fully shaded over.
setup.caption: 1. Try three big blocks first. One outbreak takes 12 plots.

setup.art: The same grid coloured in single rows of three repeating colours, with one row shaded over.
setup.caption: 2. Try rows. One outbreak takes 6 plots.

setup.art: A child rolling a die beside a new grid coloured in small pairs of three colours, with only two squares shaded.
setup.caption: 3. Draw your own plan. Roll for a row and a column and count the loss.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem aloud. 2. Draw a 6 by 6 grid and colour it in three blocks of 12. 3. Roll twice to pick a plot. Shade the plot and all joined plots of that variety. 4. Count the loss.
flow.say: Here is the easiest field to plant, in three big blocks. Roll for a row and a column. That plot falls ill. Which other plots will the fungus reach? How many is that?
flow.kid: Draw a 6 by 6 grid. Colour three blocks of 12. Roll for a row and a column. Shade that plot and all joined plots of its variety. Count them.

ask.q: Why does the whole block go?
good: Every plot in the block is the same variety and joined side to side.
It is like the pond where every snail was the same.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Mixed Field challenge. Here you test a banana field planted in three big blocks against one outbreak of a fungus.

flow.do: 1. Ask for a better plan that keeps to the rules. 2. Your child colours a new grid. 3. Check that there are 12 plots of each variety and that every plot touches one of its own. 4. Test with five outbreaks. Write each loss.
flow.say: Now plan your own field. Keep 12 plots of each variety, and let every plot touch one of its own kind. What will you change to make the loss smaller? Test it five times.
flow.kid: Colour your own field. Use 12 plots of each variety. Every plot must touch one of its own kind. Test it with five outbreaks. Write each loss.

ask.q: What is the smallest loss the rules allow, and why?
good: 2 plots. Every plot must touch one of its own variety, so the smallest group is a pair.

flow.parent: Add the five losses and divide by 5 for the average. Rows give 6 every time. A plan of pairs, with no two pairs of one variety touching, gives 2 every time. One way is to lay all pairs across the rows and repeat the colours in the order 1, 2, 3 along each row, starting one colour later in each new row.
flow.context: In this step of the Mixed Field challenge you colour your own banana field of 36 plots with three varieties and test it against five outbreaks.

flow.do: 1. Compare the average losses of blocks, rows and your child's plan. 2. Ask what the smaller groups cost the farmer. 3. Ask what else she could do over several years.
flow.say: Which plan lost least? What extra work does that plan give Lakshmi? The fungus stays in the soil for years. What could she change from year to year?
flow.kid: Compare the plans. Which lost least? What extra work does it give the farmer? What could she change each year?

check.q: Why does a field of one variety lose more to a disease than a mixed field?
options: A disease that fits one plant fits all of them
One variety always tastes worse
Mixed fields get more rain
check.why: Plants of one variety are nearly the same inside, so a fungus who can enter one can enter every neighbour. In a mixed field the fungus soon meets a plant she does not fit. Picking 'more rain' looks for a cause outside the plants, when the cause is their sameness.

flow.parent: A mixed field means more walking and sorting at harvest, and that is a real cost. This is why large farms often plant one variety, and why they are at risk.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Mixed Field challenge. Here you compare the losses of three field plans and think about what a mixed field costs the farmer.

challenges.title: Trick or Only Ill? Design a fair test by watching
challenges.context: This is a planning challenge about evidence. You design a test to find out whether a parasite changes an animal's behaviour, using only watching and counting.
challenges.problem: This case is made up. On a beach near Kochi, most small crabs stay in their burrows at noon. A few stand out on the open sand. A student finds that many of the crabs in the open carry a worm. She thinks the worm makes them stand there, so that shore birds eat them. Design a test that could show whether she is right.
constraints: You may only watch, count and gently look. No crab may be hurt or kept for more than 10 minutes.
Compare crabs who carry the worm with crabs who do not.
Use at least 20 crabs of each kind, at the same place and the same time of day.
Say beforehand what result would mean a trick, and what result would mean the crabs are only ill.
materials: your notes from the Starling Test
general: Count how many crabs with the worm, and how many without, stand in the open at noon.
Watch whether shore birds take more crabs from the open sand than from near the burrows.
Check the time. Do crabs with young worms behave normally, and only those with full-grown worms stand in the open?
creative: Time how fast each kind of crab runs to a burrow when a shadow passes. If the crabs with the worm are just as fast, they are not simply weak.
Put small clay model crabs on open sand and near burrows, and count peck marks, so that no real crab is risked.
Look at whether the change is exact. Do the crabs with the worm also feed, fight and dig as usual?
Repeat the count on a second beach, to see whether the pattern holds.
challenges.your_turn: Now write your own one-page plan with four parts: what I will compare, what I will count, what result would mean a trick, and what result would mean only ill. Then write the same four parts for an animal you can really watch, such as ants on a wall or snails after rain.

setup.art: A sandy beach at noon with many small burrow holes and three small crabs standing out on the open sand, and a shore bird in the distance.
setup.caption: 1. Read the case. A few crabs stand in the open at noon.

setup.art: A page ruled into four boxes with the headings Compare, Count, Trick if and Only ill if.
setup.caption: 2. Rule a page into four parts.

setup.art: The four boxes filled in with short handwritten notes and a small tally chart of crabs.
setup.caption: 3. Fill in your plan. Say what each result would mean.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem aloud. 2. Ask for three possible reasons why the crabs stand in the open. 3. Write each as a short line.
flow.say: The crabs in the open carry a worm. Think of three different reasons for what they do. One reason should not involve a trick at all.
flow.kid: Read the case. Think of three reasons why those crabs stand in the open. Write each one.

ask.q: What reason has nothing to do with a trick?
good: The crabs are weak and slow, and cannot dig.
Crabs who stand in the open may simply pick up more worms.

flow.parent: The second good answer is the hardest one. Standing in the open might be the cause of having worms, and not the result.
flow.context: This is the first step of Trick or Only Ill? Here you read a made-up case about crabs and think of three reasons for their behaviour.

flow.do: 1. Rule the page into four parts. 2. Your child fills in what to compare and what to count. 3. They write what result would mean a trick. 4. They write what result would mean only ill.
flow.say: What will you compare? What will you count? Now the important part. What result would tell you it is a trick? What result would tell you the crabs are only ill?
flow.kid: Rule four boxes. Write what you will compare. Write what you will count. Write what a trick would look like. Write what only ill would look like.

ask.q: Why must you say beforehand what each result would mean?
good: Otherwise any result could be made to fit the idea.
It keeps the test honest.

flow.parent: Look for a healthy group to compare with, for equal numbers, and for a check on the birds. Without birds eating more of the open crabs, there is no gain for the worm.
flow.context: In this step of Trick or Only Ill? you write a four-part plan for a fair test of whether a worm changes what crabs do.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to explain the plan aloud. 2. Ask what could still fool them. 3. They write the same four parts for an animal they can really watch.
flow.say: Tell me your plan. What could still fool you? Now choose an animal near our home, and write the four parts for a question about that animal.
flow.kid: Explain your plan. What could still fool you? Now write four parts for an animal near your home.

check.q: Crabs with the worm run to their burrows as fast as healthy crabs. What does that rule out?
options: That they stand in the open from weakness
That they carry a worm
That birds eat crabs
check.why: If they can run just as fast, they are not too weak to hide. So weakness, a side effect of illness, does not explain why they stand in the open. Picking 'that they carry a worm' mixes up what was measured, the running, with what was already known.

flow.context: This is the last step of Trick or Only Ill? Here you explain your test plan and write a new one for an animal you can watch near home.

worksheets.title: Hosts, parasites and the race between them

items.p: Which of these is a parasite?
opts: A louse feeding on a scalp
A crow eating a grain of rice
A bee visiting a flower
items.why: A louse lives on another living being and takes food from them. A crow eating rice and a bee at a flower do not live on or in a host.

items.p: The living being that a parasite lives on or in is called the ____.
items.why: The host gives the parasite food and a home. A person is the host of a head louse, and a snail is the host of a young fluke.

items.p: In an arms race between a host and a parasite, one side wins for good.
items.why: False. Each defence is followed by a way round it, and then by a new defence. Neither side stays ahead, because both keep changing.

items.p: Match each move to the other side's answer.
pairs: Cuckoos lay eggs that look like the host's
The body makes antibodies to a coat
The parasite switches to a new coat
Rare kinds of snail take over
items.why: In each pair the second line only makes sense as an answer to the first. That is what an arms race looks like: a move, and then a move that gets round it.

items.p: Each fluke fits one kind of snail. Which kind of snail is infected most?
opts: The commonest kind
The rarest kind
All kinds equally
items.why: Flukes who fit the commonest snail find hosts most easily and have the most young. So most flukes come to fit the commonest snail. Choosing 'all kinds equally' treats the flukes as fixed, but they change with the snails.

items.p: Sort each behaviour by who gains from it.
items: A mantis with a hairworm walking into water
A lizard with an infection basking longer
A rat with Toxoplasma walking towards cat smell
An ant with a fungus biting a leaf at midday
items.why: Preening, basking and grooming remove or slow parasites. The mantis, the rat and the ant each do something that carries the parasite to the place or the host needed next.

items.p: Put these in order, from first to last, for a body meeting a new parasite.
items: That cell divides into thousands of copies
One white blood cell's antibody fits the parasite
Antibodies mark the parasites to be destroyed
a: One white blood cell's antibody fits the parasite
That cell divides into thousands of copies
Antibodies mark the parasites to be destroyed
items.why: The body does not design an antibody. It already has many kinds, and the one that fits is copied. Memory cells make the second meeting much faster.

items.p: A bite from a pet dog never needs a doctor.
items.why: False. Nobody can tell by looking whether a dog carries rabies. Wash any bite or scratch for 15 minutes, tell a grown-up and see a doctor the same day.

items.p: When parasites survive a medicine that used to kill their kind, this is called ____.
items.why: The medicine kills the others, and the few who survive leave the young. After some years most parasites are of the surviving kind.

items.p: A hairworm grows inside a mantis but must mate in water. What is the hairworm's problem?
opts: The worm cannot cross dry ground alone
The worm is afraid of the mantis
The mantis lives under water
items.why: A hairworm has no legs and would dry out on land. The mantis has legs. The mantis walking to water solves the worm's problem.

items.p: A pond holds only one kind of snail, all clones. Explain why one kind of fluke could empty it.
items.a: Every snail has the same lock, so a fluke who fits one snail fits them all. That fluke has many young, and soon most snails are infected. There is no rare kind of snail left to carry on.
items.why: A strong answer says that the snails are all alike, and that there is no rare kind for the flukes to miss.

items.p: Label the four steps to take after a dog bite, in order.
a: Wash with soap and running water for 15 minutes
See a doctor the same day
Take every dose of the vaccine
items.why: The virus travels slowly along the nerves, so there is time to stop the virus. Washing removes much of the virus, and the vaccine readies the body before the virus reaches the brain.
items.art: Four empty boxes in a row joined by arrows, with small faint drawings of a tap, a parent, a doctor and a calendar above them.

items.p: Draw a line graph of three kinds of snail over eight generations, when flukes chase the commonest kind.
items.a: Three lines that rise and fall in turn. When one line is highest it soon drops, and a line that was low rises. The lines cross at least once.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that no line stays on top. The commonest kind is infected most, so a rare kind takes over.
items.art: Blank axes on squared paper, with Generation 1 to 8 along the bottom and Number of snails 0 to 12 up the side.

items.p: Should people try to wipe out every kind of parasite?

views.says: Yes. Parasites make millions of people ill, and children suffer most.
No. Parasites feed fish and birds and stop any one animal from taking over.

views.who: A doctor who has seen Guinea worm
views.says: Remove the few who harm people most, and leave the rest alone.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from what you have learned. Then answer back one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. A strong answer separates parasites who cause great human suffering, such as the Guinea worm and the malaria parasite, from the many who are part of lakes and forests.
items.why: This question has no single right answer. What matters is a reason that uses evidence, and a fair reply to another view.

items.p: A parasite doubles every day. On day 1 there is 1. How many are there on day 6?
items.why: The numbers go 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. Doubling five times gives 32. This is why a body has only a few days to learn a new coat.

worksheets.title: Coats, medicines and parasites who steer

items.p: Why can most parasites change faster than their hosts?
opts: Parasites have new generations much more often
Parasites are cleverer than hosts
Hosts never change at all
items.why: Change spreads from one generation to the next. A parasite may have a new generation in days and a host in years. Hosts do change, but more slowly.

items.p: An antibody made for one coat of a parasite grips every other coat too.
items.why: False. Each antibody fits one shape. When the parasite switches coat, the body must start learning again.

items.p: Three of these are a host's defences. Which is the odd one out?
opts: Preening
Fever
Coat changing
Grooming
items.why: Coat changing is a parasite's move against antibodies. Preening, fever and grooming are all things a host does against parasites.

items.p: Sort these claims by how strong the evidence is.
items: Starlings ate more infected pill bugs
Cats catch more infected rats outdoors
Infected mantises walk towards light from water
A Guinea worm's blister sends people to water
Dogs with rabies bite more than other dogs
items.why: A claim is tested when someone has compared infected and healthy hosts fairly and counted. The three untested claims fit what we know, but nobody has made the comparison.

items.p: Birds took 2 of every 100 healthy fish. They took infected fish 10 times as often. How many of 100 infected fish?
items.why: 2 times 10 is 20. In the real study birds took infected killifish 10 to 30 times as often, so the number could be as high as 60.

items.p: A sneeze clears your nose and also spreads a cold virus. What is the fairest conclusion?
opts: It may serve both you and the virus
It serves only the virus
It serves only you
items.why: The sneeze does two things at once. Scientists still argue about how much of it is defence and how much helps the virus. One behaviour can serve two living beings.

items.p: Put these in order, from first to last.
items: A few parasites survive the medicine
a: A few parasites survive the medicine
items.why: The medicine removes the ordinary parasites, so the few who survive leave the young. Two medicines together are much harder to get round.

items.p: The idea that living beings must keep changing just to stay as safe as before is the ____ idea.
items.why: It is named after the Red Queen in Through the Looking-Glass, who tells Alice that here you must run as fast as you can to stay in the same place.

items.p: Match each parasite to what the parasite needs next.
pairs: A leaf above the ants' path
items.why: In each case the host's changed behaviour takes the parasite to exactly this place. That close fit is one sign of manipulation.

items.p: Scientists have found the zombie-ant fungus growing all through the ant's brain.
items.why: False. In 2017 the fungus was found around and inside the muscles, and was not found inside the brain. How the ant is steered is still unknown.

items.p: Pill bugs with a worm inside moved about more than healthy ones. Why did that matter?
items.a: It showed that the infected pill bugs were not simply weak or tired. A weak animal moves less. Their behaviour had changed in a particular way that took them into the open.
items.why: A strong answer says that more movement rules out the old idea that infected animals only behave oddly from weakness.

items.p: Explain why stopping a medicine early helps resistant parasites.
items.a: The first tablets kill the parasites that are easiest to kill. The toughest ones are still alive. If the medicine stops, they multiply and are passed on.
items.why: A strong answer says that an unfinished course removes the easy parasites and leaves the tough ones to have young.

items.p: A mantis with a hairworm inside walks into a pond. Whose walk is it?

views.says: The mantis's. Her legs did the walking, so she did it.
The worm's. Only the worm needed the water.
Both. Neither could have made that walk alone.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from what you have learned. Then answer back one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. A strong answer uses the evidence: healthy mantises do not walk to water, the walk begins only when the worm is full grown, and the worm has no legs.
items.why: This question has no single right answer. What matters is a reason that uses the evidence, and a fair reply to another view.

items.p: Label the three parts of this picture of a body meeting a parasite.
labels: The outer layer that it grips
The cell that stays for years
items.why: An antibody grips the coat. A memory cell keeps the pattern, so that the same coat is answered within days next time.
items.art: A round parasite with a beaded outline, a Y shape gripping the outline, and a round white blood cell nearby, with three empty label lines.

items.p: Which is true of a koel chick in a crow's nest?
opts: The koel chick grows up beside the crow chicks
The koel chick is fed by the koel mother
The koel chick builds a new nest
items.why: The koel mother lays the egg and leaves. The crows feed the koel chick together with their own chicks. The koel chick does not push the crow chicks out.

worksheets.title: Testing, arguing and working it out

items.p: Animals with a parasite sit in the open. What must be shown before calling it the parasite's trick?
opts: More of them reach the parasite's next host
They look unusual
They are thinner than the others
items.why: A change is manipulation only if it carries more parasites onward. Looking unusual or being thin could be side effects of illness.

items.p: In a hunting test with paper bugs, which round is the control?
opts: All bugs hide in the same way
Dotted bugs stand in the open
The hunter uses both hands
items.why: In the control nothing differs between the two groups, so it shows whether the dot alone matters. It did not. Only the place did.

items.p: If a claim fits everything we know, it has been tested.
items.why: False. Fitting is not testing. A claim is tested when someone compares and counts, and the result could have come out the other way.

items.p: A pond has 12 clone snails. Two thirds are infected. Each healthy snail has one baby. How many snails are there now?
items.why: Two thirds of 12 is 8 infected, so 4 are healthy. Each has one baby, and 4 plus 4 is 8. The pond has shrunk from 12 to 8 in one generation.

items.p: A model parasite shows a new coat every 4 days and has 60 coats. How many days can the infection last?
items.why: 60 times 4 is 240 days, which is about 8 months. A real malaria parasite has about 60 genes for their marker protein, and infections can last many months.

items.p: Why might any effect of Toxoplasma on people be a leftover?
opts: Cats almost never eat people
People cannot carry the parasite
The parasite mates in people
items.why: The parasite gains when a rat is eaten by a cat. A person will not be eaten by a cat, so a change in a person carries the parasite nowhere. It may be left over from what works in rats.

items.p: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: An exact copy of one parent
The part of a test where nothing is changed
The host where a parasite has young
A change that helps nobody in particular
items.why: These four words are needed to talk about the arms race and about testing. A control and a side effect are the two that people most often forget.

items.p: Put a hairworm's journey in order, from first to last.
items: The worm leaves and mates in water
The mantis walks to shining water
A mantis eats an insect carrying a young worm
The worm grows until the mantis's body is nearly full
a: A mantis eats an insect carrying a young worm
The worm grows until the mantis's body is nearly full
The mantis walks to shining water
The worm leaves and mates in water
items.why: The mantis is drawn to water only once the worm is full grown. A change that begins exactly when the parasite is ready is one sign of manipulation.

items.p: Light that bounces off flat water has waves lying in one direction. It is called ____ light.
items.why: Mantises with a hairworm inside walked towards this light in a test in Japan in 2021. Healthy mantises did not.

items.p: Rats with Toxoplasma lost their fear of cat smell but kept their other fears. Why does that matter?
items.a: If the rats were only ill, all their behaviour would be dulled. Losing one exact fear, the one that keeps them away from the parasite's final host, points to a particular change and not general illness.
items.why: A strong answer says that an exact change is unlikely to be a mere side effect of feeling ill.

items.p: Some snails sit on top of leaves in daylight. Plan a test of whether a parasite causes this.
items.a: Compare snails who carry the parasite with snails who do not, in the same place and at the same time. Count how many of each sit on top of leaves. Then count whether birds take more snails from the leaf tops. Say beforehand what result would mean a trick.
items.why: A strong answer has a comparison with healthy snails, a count, and a check that the change helps the parasite reach the next host.

items.p: Draw a graph of parasites in the blood for a coat-changing parasite. Mark where the body has learned a coat.
items.a: A line that rises, drops sharply, rises again and drops again, in several waves. An arrow at each drop is labelled: the body has learned this coat.
items.why: A strong drawing shows waves, with each fall caused by new antibodies and each rise caused by a parasite in a new coat.
items.art: Blank axes with Days along the bottom and Parasites in the blood up the side.

items.p: Hosts and parasites have changed each other for millions of years. Is this a war?

views.says: Yes. Parasites harm us and we fight to be rid of them.
No. Neither side can end the other, and each keeps the other varied.
War is a human word. The snails and flukes are only living.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from what you have learned. Then answer back one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. A strong answer notices that in a war one side hopes to end the other, and that in the pond the flukes die out if the snails do.
items.why: This question has no single right answer. What matters is a reason that uses the evidence, and a fair reply to another view.

items.p: A field with several varieties usually loses less to one disease than a field of one variety.
items.why: True. A disease that fits one variety is stopped when the next plant is a different variety. It is the same reason that the mixed pond lasted longer than the clone pond.

items.p: Sort these host defences.
items.why: Hosts defend themselves with their bodies and with their behaviour. Because behaviour is a defence, a parasite who can change behaviour gains a great deal.

quiz.p: Which best describes an arms race between a host and a parasite?
opts: Each side keeps changing in answer to the other
The host changes and the parasite stays the same
The stronger side wins and it ends
quiz.why: Each defence is followed by a way round it. Choosing 'the stronger side wins' misses that neither side stays ahead, because both keep changing.

quiz.p: A medicine against a parasite is used widely. After years it works less well. Why?
opts: Parasites who survive it left the young
The tablets became weaker
People's bodies got used to it
quiz.why: The medicine removes the ordinary parasites. The few who can survive it multiply. The tablets and the people have not changed. The parasites have.

quiz.p: Flukes each fit one kind of snail. One kind of snail becomes very common. What happens next?
opts: Flukes who fit that kind multiply, and it goes down
That kind stays on top for ever
The flukes die out
quiz.why: Being common makes a snail kind the easiest host to find, so her flukes do best. Choosing 'stays on top for ever' treats the flukes as fixed.

quiz.p: Why is a group of clones in more danger from a parasite than a mixed group?
opts: A parasite who fits one clone fits them all
Clones are always smaller
Clones cannot have young
quiz.why: Clones are copies, so they share the same locks. A mixed group always has some rare kind that few parasites fit.

opts: Grips one particular shape on a germ or parasite
Carries oxygen in the blood
Kills every microbe nearby
quiz.why: An antibody is a Y-shaped protein that fits one shape only. It marks the parasite for other cells to destroy. It does not fit every microbe.

quiz.p: How does a coat-changing parasite stay in the blood for months?
opts: Some switch to a coat the body has not learned
They hide in the stomach
They stop multiplying
quiz.why: Antibodies clear one coat, but a few parasites have already switched to another. The body has to start learning again, so the numbers rise and fall in waves.

quiz.p: A fluke must get from a fish into a bird. Which change in the fish helps the fluke?
opts: The fish flashes near the surface
The fish hides in deep weed
The fish swims faster from birds
quiz.why: A fish who flashes near the surface is easier for a bird to see and catch. Birds ate infected killifish 10 to 30 times as often as healthy ones.

quiz.p: A mantis with a full-grown hairworm inside walks into water. Who needs the water?
opts: The hairworm, who mates in water
The mantis, who is thirsty
Neither of them
quiz.why: Adult hairworms live and mate in water. Healthy mantises keep away from water. Choosing 'the mantis is thirsty' does not explain why only infected mantises do it.

quiz.p: An ill goat lies still all day. What must be shown before calling this a parasite's trick?
opts: That lying still helps the parasite spread
That the goat has a parasite
That the goat looks unhappy
quiz.why: Lying still could be a side effect of being weak, or the goat saving strength. It is a trick only if the change carries more parasites to the next host.

quiz.p: Every odd behaviour of an infected animal is caused by the parasite to help the parasite.
quiz.why: False. Some odd behaviours are the host's own defence, such as a fever or basking in the sun. Some are side effects of illness. Each case has to be tested.

quiz.p: Which of these claims do scientists still argue about?
opts: Toxoplasma changes human personality
Infected rats lose their fear of cat smell
Birds eat more infected killifish
quiz.why: The rat and killifish findings were tested by comparing infected and healthy animals. Studies of people and Toxoplasma disagree with each other.

quiz.p: A dog's tooth scratches your hand and breaks the skin. What do you do first?
opts: Wash with soap and running water for 15 minutes
Cover it with turmeric
Wait to see if the dog falls ill
quiz.why: Washing at once removes much of the virus. Then tell a grown-up and see a doctor the same day. Waiting is dangerous, because rabies cannot be cured once signs begin.

quiz.p: You can catch Toxoplasma by stroking a healthy cat's fur.
quiz.why: False. The parasite is passed in cat dung and gets into soil, sand and unwashed vegetables. Wash your hands after touching soil or a litter tray, and wash vegetables.

applications: Malaria programmes give two medicines together and watch for places where a medicine has begun to work less well, so that the parasites cannot get round one medicine at a time.
Farmers mix varieties, change crops from year to year and keep old varieties as seed, so that one disease cannot run through a whole district.
Doctors prevent rabies after a bite by washing the wound and giving the vaccine, using the weeks that the virus needs to travel along the nerves.
Vaccine makers study which parts of a parasite's surface cannot be changed easily, and aim vaccines at those parts.
Scientists turned CRISPR, the defence that bacteria use against viruses, into a tool for changing genes in plants, animals and people.
People who protect rare animals keep many unrelated families, because a small group of near-copies is easily wiped out by one disease.
Health workers treat whole villages for worms at the same time, so that the worms have no untreated host to wait in.

open_questions.q: How does the zombie-ant fungus steer an ant?
open_questions.why_open: The fungus was found in the muscles and was not found inside the brain. Nobody knows whether the fungus works the muscles directly or sends chemicals to the brain.

open_questions.q: Does Toxoplasma change how people behave?
open_questions.why_open: Some studies find small differences in infected people and others find none. Infected and uninfected people differ in many other ways too, which are hard to separate.

open_questions.q: Is the chase between hosts and parasites the main reason that most animals and plants have two parents?
open_questions.why_open: It has been shown in some snails. But some clones have lasted a very long time, and other explanations fit other animals better.

open_questions.q: What is it like to be a host whose behaviour a parasite has changed?
open_questions.why_open: We can measure what a mantis does. We have no way yet to find out whether the pull towards water feels to the mantis like her own wish.

open_questions.q: Do crows have any defence against koels?
open_questions.why_open: Nobody has yet tested how often crows throw out strange eggs, and the 2021 study found no close copying of crow eggs by koels.

open_questions.q: Did the mitochondria in our cells begin as parasites?
open_questions.why_open: They were once free-living bacteria. Whether the first ones entered a larger cell as food, as guests or as parasites happened too long ago to see directly.

open_questions.q: Can a medicine or vaccine be made that parasites cannot get round?
open_questions.why_open: Every medicine so far has met resistance in the end. Scientists are looking for parts of a parasite that cannot change without killing the parasite.
